entries.title: Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong wins NL MVP to cap all-time season of homers, stolen bases and defensive excellence
entries.summary: <p>Pete Crow-Armstrong is the National League’s Most Valuable Player.</p><p>But you didn’t need Thursday’s official announcement to know that.</p><p>All you had to do was be one of the many who marveled at all the 24-year-old <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> superstar did on the field this season to know there was no one in the sport who had as much of an impact as he did.</p><p>“Watching him every day,” starting pitcher Shota Imanaga said through an interpreter in mid June, “he’s a player that overcomes your imagination.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong has a full trophy case in the wake of one of baseball’s all-time great individual campaigns, just the seventh 40-homer, 40-steal season in major league history with Platinum Glove defense, to boot.</p><p>He’s the Cubs’ first MVP since Kris Bryant took home the award in 2016, the same year his team won the World Series. He’s the 12th player to win an MVP as a Cub, joining legends such as Sammy Sosa, Andre Dawson, Ryne Sandberg and Ernie Banks.</p><p>But unlike all those household names at Clark and Addison, Crow-Armstrong did it in a way that hadn’t been done before. That’s what had teammates in awe all summer long.</p><p>More than the numbers, Crow-Armstrong provided one signature moment after another. He delivered walk-off wins, multi-homer games, a cycle and a memorable night with fellow Chicago sports stars in attendance.</p><p>He also duked it out with Dodgers two-way superstar Shohei Ohtani, the man no one believed could be dethroned from his status as the perennial MVP. That Crow-Armstrong’s win comes in the Ohtani Era is even more impressive, even with Ohtani’s injury issues keeping him from his best self this year.</p><p>For a while, though, there was a real argument that Crow-Armstrong, with his offensive and defensive prowess, matched Ohtani’s impact as both an elite hitter and an elite pitcher.</p><p>“It is really similar to what I saw last year,” designated hitter Michael Conforto, who played with Ohtani in 2025 and Crow-Armstrong in 2026, said in September. “You see a guy go out there and do things that no one else can do. And he does it different than Shohei does it. But it’s the same thing. He moves differently. He has different tools than everyone else.</p><p>“You just kind of enjoy sitting back and watching history being made.”</p><p>It was a remarkable transformation that launched Crow-Armstrong into the stratosphere of baseball’s greats. A guy who chased pitches out of the zone and slumped badly in the second half of the 2025 season was a changed hitter in 2026, his on-base percentage skyrocketing from .287 to .372 and his walk rate shooting up from 4.5 percent to 11.4 as newfound patience made him one of the game’s most dangerous batsmen.</p><p>Add the base-running and defensive abilities that were always there, and the Cubs have a player at the top of their lineup who makes an all-around impact unlike any other in the sport.</p><p>“The most impressive thing is the plate discipline and the walks,” outfielder Ian Happ said in early July. “For him to get to this point this quickly and really … kind of change the way that he approaches at-bats and the patience, the ability to lay off some really tough pitches … that’s been the most impressive thing to watch.</p><p>“There’s always been thump there. There’s always been unbelievable tools and the speed and the defense. … But … to watch the way that he’s walking, it makes him so lethal because he’s such a good baserunner.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong spent the summer downplaying individual accomplishments, choosing to focus on team goals. At times, he waved away impressive feats, zeroing in on what he could have done better.</p><p>So it’s no surprise that on the night he won the MVP, he was thinking along those lines.</p><p>“In the most humble way I can say it, I still don’t feel satisfied with the product that I put on the field this year,” he said Thursday. “It sounds so melancholy, but I’m so happy being able to say this because I know there’s more.</p><p>“This is definitely a huge accomplishment of mine, this award, but success in my eyes is being called a winner. And I’m not necessarily there yet.</p><p>“Hopefully, I can be talking to you as a World Series champion and MVP.”</p>

entries.title: Finalists for Chicago's next top cop are all CPD insiders
entries.summary: <p>Three high-ranking Chicago police officials were picked as finalists to replace former Supt. Larry Snelling, including a candidate who, if selected, would be the first woman to ever lead the department.</p><p>First Deputy Supt. Antoinette Ursitti, Chief of Community Policing Angel Novalez and Counterterrorism Chief Christopher Papaioannou were the choices of the commission tasked with conducting a nationwide search for the city’s new top cop. </p><p>The Community Commission for Public Safety and Accountability voted Thursday evening to send the names to Mayor Brandon Johnson, starting a 30-day clock for him to make a pick or reject all three candidates and request a second search.</p><p>The city paid national search firm Ralph Andersen & Associates $200,000 to assist the commission. The search drew 46 candidates, down slightly from the 2023 cycle when 53 people applied for the job.</p><p>The applicants included current and former members of the Chicago Police Department, along with law enforcement officials from across the country</p><p>"Having gone through this before, we understand just how much leadership matters," Remel Terry, the commission president, told reporters after the meeting. </p><p>"The right superintendent can shape the direction and culture of the entire department and make a real difference in how public safety is delivered across Chicago. We know what's possible under strong leadership, and we understand what's at stake in getting the decision right."</p><p>Commissioner Angelique Guzman was the sole "no" vote against Papaioannou's nomination. She later said "given current times and the current federal administration," she did not believe he was the best candidate for superintendent. </p><h3><b>Antoinette Ursitti</b></h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-9a0000" name="image-9a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/67ef7d6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6787x3809+0+359/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb7%2F62%2Fc1f2eb7ac939832ad3316119f2b9%2F7935-x143-4b33-7.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0139c9f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6787x3809+0+359/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb7%2F62%2Fc1f2eb7ac939832ad3316119f2b9%2F7935-x143-4b33-7.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bad3153/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6787x3809+0+359/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb7%2F62%2Fc1f2eb7ac939832ad3316119f2b9%2F7935-x143-4b33-7.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Chicago Police Supt. Before that, she spent three years as chief of detectives, overseeing a rise in clearance rates.</p><p>She stands out among her peers for having returned to school not just to earn a masters degree but also a doctorate decree. She is also a licensed counselor in Illinois.</p><p>In announcing her promotion to first deputy superintendent, the police department described her as “a purpose-driven leader who prioritizes the entries.title: Michael Reese developers pitch $10 billion stadium project to lure Bears
entries.summary: <p>A team of Chicago developers unveiled Thursday a $10 billion, 100-acre development plan for the former Michael Reese Hospital site — both as a Hail Mary to keep the Bears in Chicago and to hit a city-imposed deadline to submit updated plans. </p><p>The Bears previously <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/bears-stadium/2024/05/16/bears-stadium-lakefront-soldier-field-michael-reese-hospital-site-civic-federation-kevin-warren" >dismissed</a> the Michael Reese site, saying it was too narrow and posed safety concerns because the stadium would have to be built over an active rail line.</p><p>But with Capri Investment Group founder Quintin Primo joining GRIT Chicago, the group of developers and investors led by Farpoint Development that purchased the Michael Reese site, the partners have nearly doubled the size of the proposed Bronzeville Lakefront development. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f80000" name="image-f80000"></a> Primo III, founder and executive chairman of Capri Investment Group, speaks during a press conference at Olivet Baptist Church. He unveiled a new Bronzeville Lakefront development plan that would transform the former Michael Reese Hospital site into a sports, entertainment and cultural district anchored by a potential Bears stadium.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>They shared grand plans to redevelop a large portion of the South Side into a sports, entertainment and cultural district that would, of course, be anchored by a domed stadium at the widest portion of the trapezoid-shaped site.</p><p>To further lure the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a>, Capri and its investment partners said they were willing to purchase the team's Arlington Heights property. It’s “the key impediment to the team staying Downtown and fairly considering Bronzeville,” Primo said.</p><p>“There should be absolutely no reasons why the Bears and the NFL should not seriously consider Bronzeville Lakefront as the best site for their new home,” he said during a Thursday press conference.</p><p>When asked if the updated plans were shared with the Bears, McLaurin Development Partners founder and CEO Zeb McLaurin said the team will leave “no stone unturned” when it comes to communicating the benefits of the site.</p><p>A Bears spokesperson declined to comment.</p><p>Renderings by Chicago-based design firm Studio Inference show a glassy 75,000-seat stadium that would host the Bears in addition to other sporting events and concerts. High-rise and mid-rise buildings surround the stadium, along with a sprawling public park, event stage and youth sports complex, among other features.</p><p>“It is our belief that a modern, competitive dome stadium such as the one we are proposing will outperform suburban locations such as Arlington Heights or Northwest Indiana,” Primo said. “This is just plain common sense, in our opinion, as these remote locations are not at the heart of the most important economic driver of the entire Midwest.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" >Prairie Shores</a>, along King Drive between 26th and 31st streets. The property is owned by Golub & Co., who initially purchased it with Farpoint for an estimated $180 million in 2019. </p><p>Golub didn’t respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Plans call for demolishing up to 1,000 units at Prairie Shores during Phase 1 and building about 1,500 apartments. The developers said they would build 1.5 replacement apartments for every existing unit that’s demolished.</p><p>Fourth Ward Ald. Lamont Robinson represents the South Side ward that includes the Michael Reese site, once purchased by the city for an Olympic Village that was never built after the 2016 Summer Games were awarded to Rio de Janeiro.</p><p>“I want to be very clear that before you can remove, tear down Prairie Shores, you have to put the units up first. You need to have 1,000 units up before you can take one unit down or have one family displaced,” Robinson told the Chicago Sun-Times. “You have to have someone that is stewarding this. And the commitment is, before you can bring any housing down, you have to have the new property up. That is a commitment that this developer has made.”</p><p>The developers are also proposing a community benefits agreement that would give "priority treatment for affected households to reside in new housing within the district or nearby, rent protections for five years, additional assistance for longer-term residents and oversight by a resident committee and independent monitor."</p><div Ellis Ave. in Bronzeville, where developers have proposed a sports, entertainment and cultural district anchored by a potential Bears stadium.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In total, more than 5,000 homes are expected to be built on-site and in nearby locations, including affordable, senior and student housing. The plan cited Lake Meadows as a potential housing site as well as "early discussions" with Illinois Tech to build on-campus housing.</p><p>It also proposed air rights over the McCormick Place Marshaling Yard to the east and expanding McCormick Place's convention and meeting spaces by 300,000 square feet.</p><p>The Metropolitan Pier and Exposition Authority, which owns McCormick Place, said it supports efforts to boost Chicago's economy.</p><p>"However, the Authority must follow its governing mission as well as adhere to its legislatively mandated procurement procedures. The proposed Bronzeville project may offer interesting opportunities for Chicago, but it is in its early stages. MPEA looks forward to learning more about the plans and discussing it with our clients and community stakeholders. At this time, the Authority has not made any commitments related to the project," an MPEA spokesperson said in a statement.</p><p>What sets the development apart from others attempting to woo the Bears, the developers said, is that the new stadium will be joined by hotels, recreational facilities and housing that would <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/11/25/chicago-architecture-center-report-urban-stadiums-development" >bring an economic boon</a> to Bronzeville.</p><p>The developers estimate housing, hotels, retail and commercial uses could generate about $135 million in annual tax revenue. They also project about $14 billion in regional economic activity during its development, with about 60,000 construction-related jobs.</p><h3>Second chance</h3><p>If the Michael Reese stadium plan has a familiar ring to it, it should.</p><p>In March 2025, developers of the former hospital site went public with a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/bears-stadium/2025/03/14/bears-stadium-michael-reese-proposal-scott-goodman" >dazzling Hail Mary plan</a> to build a $3.2 billion Bronzeville stadium and an adjacent mixed-use development — with a great lawn extending over Du Sable Lake Shore Drive all the way to Lake Michigan.</p><p>Scott Goodman, principal of Farpoint Development, acknowledged then that he had not met with the Bears, nor had he finalized the financing for the dome or the $600 million in state money needed just to ready the site for development. </p><p>The previous stadium construction cost, estimated at $3.2 billion, was the same amount the Bears assumed in 2024 when team president Kevin Warren <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/04/23/bears-new-stadium-dome-lakefront-soldier-field" target="_blank" >stood with Mayor Brandon Johnson to unveil their preferred lakefront stadium proposal</a> on the Museum Campus — a plan that got stuck in the mud in Springfield and could face legal challenges due to the city’s lakefront protection ordinance.</p><p>Robinson acknowledged the Bears long ago dismissed the Michael Reese site. But he’s all for the idea of including it in the salad bar of Chicago stadium sites for the Bears to consider, along with the site they already own in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/06/bears-stadium-roger-goodell-nfl-commissioner-george-mccaskey-kevin-warren-chicago-arlington-heights-meeting-hammond-indiana" target="_blank" >Arlington Heights</a>.</p><p>“As the alderman of the 4th Ward, I have to develop this site. I cannot leave this site dormant for another 20 years,” Robinson said. “We need more housing, and we need to put this back on the rolls for taxes. The city needs resources and we need housing. As the Bears have stated, they are still looking at sites, and why would we not put everything on the table and have the Bears look at it?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div We’d be open to having those conversations,” Robinson said, acknowledging the White Sox and the Stars as possibilities.</p><p>Without an anchor like a stadium, Robinson said the Michael Reese development could remain bogged down with another city deadline looming. GRIT has until Dec. 14 to submit an updated infrastructure plan for the site as part of the Bronzeville Lakefront redevelopment process. The development team said it’s preparing a new infrastructure plan to submit to the city and the proposal will continue to be refined with stakeholders, including the Bears.</p><p>“That’s why this plan is out. So many folks can look at it and decide if they’re interested in the site,” Robinson said. “We can’t just do nothing. We have to put plans out there … We gotta develop it. We’ve got to get this thing moving.”</p><p>Bronzeville Lakefront would be a massive public-private undertaking and comes days before lawmakers in Springfield consider financing tools that could sweeten the deal for the Bears to stay in Illinois, making it the perfect time to announce the new plans, McLaurin said.</p><p>State Sen. Willie Preston recalled walking his grandmother to the train, where she’d put in her train token to go to work at Michael Reese Hospital, before urging public officials during Thursday's news conference to act in favor of the Bronzeville site.</p><p>“What you all have created and provided, this development team, is a token to get on the train,” Preston said. “So I’m asking Mayor Brandon Johnson, my good friend Gov. JB Pritzker, the McCaskey family: Take this token and get on the train to economic development ... [and] economic prosperity for the South Side of Chicago.”</p><p>Capri and GRIT's plan envisions a publicly owned stadium similar to Allegiant Stadium, home of the Raiders. Allegiant is owned by the Las Vegas Stadium Authority and was partially taxpayer-funded through a hotel room tax.</p><p>The developers said the Bears could help foot the bill through the sale of stadium naming rights and personal seat licenses, NFL financing programs and refinancing and issuing Illinois Sports Facilities Authority bonds. It would also count on a mix of municipal, state and federal dollars, as well as tax increment financing, sales tax-backed bonds and transportation funding.</p><p>The development team also said it recently signed a memorandum of understanding with "a major capital provider." </p><p>“We have had some very good conversations with capital partners, global organizations, who understand the virtue of how important sports and sports economic development is,” McLaurin said. “We’ve educated them all about the aspects, of the uniqueness of the Bronzeville community, our connectivity, which has been well discussed here today. entries.title: It's been 30 years, but this movie is still my 'Jam'
entries.summary: <p>Jim Riswold, the creative director and writer of the famous “Hare Jordan” Super Bowl commercial by Nike and Widen + Kennedy in 1992 that put Bugs Bunny and Michael Jordan together explained his reasoning behind the ad like this: “I couldn’t think of a bigger star to team [Jordan] up with than Bugs Bunny.”</p><p>Forward four years, we kinda all know what happened next.</p><p>This Sunday marks the 30th Anniversary of the seminal film experience called “Space Jam.” The highest-grossing American basketball film (or film centered around basketball) of all time. The singular, stand-alone vehicle that elevated Jordan into a stratosphere above any layer of fame any athlete had ever been and turned Bugs into the one thing he’d never been: a movie star.</p><p>An inspired by true events (MJ making fun of, providing levity to his real life/professional saga), over-simplistic kids movie that catered to the child-nature and obsession adults at the time had (still have) over Jordan that over time turned into something that exceeded cult-classic status.</p><p>One of those “things” that over the run of its existence transcended everything it was intended to be. It found an audience and in it the audience found depth. It found aspiration and inspiration.</p><p>We too drank “Michael’s Secret Stuff.”</p><p>Howard “H” White, Jordan’s Yoda, long-standing Nike executive who was on the set with Jordan while filming “Space Jam,” furthered then’s truth. “‘M’ grew up with Bugs Bunny. Hero. I remember in a conversation someone said to him, ‘That’s easy for you to say, you’re Michael Jordan’ and he responded, ‘Well I haven’t always been this.’ In movies? Do you think he thought he was going to be this? But you never know what you can be, not even him. He knew the one thing you can’t do is stop believing in what you can be before you ever get there.</p><p>“He never let anything deter him from what he was trying to create.”</p><p>The advanced technology of live-action film and the ability to manipulate the virtual aspect of film back then (with the exception of “Roger Rabbit”) was revolutionary. The co-existence of everything currently Jordan with everything historic to Bugs became an appetency come true.</p><p>Add to the fact that by the film’s release Jordan had come back to the NBA and won what would be the first of the Bulls’ second three-peat creating an almost biblical BC/AD dividing line of his basketball career. Jordan pre-shooting “Space Jam” versus Jordan after finishing “Space Jam” became the poor people’s ‘‘First Take’’ debate that was closer to the core of accuracy then anything anyone at ESPN would talk about.</p><p>Post-“Girl 6” Theresa Randall. Larry Bird and Patrick Ewing with personalities. Newman acting against type playing Jordan’s Stan. Danny DeVito as Red Auerbach, my bad, Mr. Swackhammer. Nerdlucks-turned-Monstars preluding the original Minions. Only thing missing: David Stern playing David Stern in the actual movie.</p><p>From a sneaker culture perspective, the film still to this day remains famed. The fight between the AJ IX that Jordan practiced in when he was first sucked down into Looney Land and the all-black AJ XI that literally became one of the most grail’d sneakers in the history of the game due to the fact that the ones he wore in the film weren’t released until four years after the movie came out.</p><p>The Jordan Brand and Warner Bros. decided to collaborate to make sure the film gets the 30th celebration it has earned. Invite-only, interactive events in LA and NYC; celebrity-hosted discussions with major-players in the music, fashion, film, sports and entertainment worlds; an upgraded product line rooted in the original merchandise that gives 30-year-old fits a whole next life.</p><p>As Jordan Brand senior manager Terrance Harvey explained to me, “ ‘Space Jam,’ MJ’s legacy and everything connected to it, has really shaped this culture that we love. They gave me the opportunity to dream, to believe. I was 2-years-old when the movie came out, too young to even understand what was going on, to even see MJ play. But just to have something that transcended time for 30 years resonated. When I saw the film for the first time, seeing MJ stretch his arm to score at the end, it gave me hope.”</p><p>Hope that don’t stop as there’s also a six-part “Beyond The Jam” YouTube mini-doc headed our way to keep the fascination fresh, but not to death. Just enough to recapture the nostalgia that once was. Tap into our “still is.” Extend the film’s three-decade placebo effect.</p><p>Multiple releases and re-releases on VHS, DVD, Blu-Ray over the post-box office years. It was one of those movies that destroyed too many VHS rewind buttons. A soundtrack that stacked bangers and is still considered one of the most iconic urban/pop/dance soundtracks ever. A merchandising and product behemoth, a commercial appeal case study, a historical incubator of all things and everything 90’s.</p><p>Until someone decided to make a sequel.</p><p>Funny how you can turn $80M into $250M ($520M adjusted to 2026) and multi-billions worth of influence when you attach a couple of global icons to a project and change the landscape of basketball, film, marketing, merchandising, music, sneaker and pop culture at the same time. As Bugs said at the end of the original commercial: “This could be the beginning of a beautiful friendship.”</p><p>Hella genius Easter egg, ya’ think?</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks maintain structure, end skid by rallying past Sabres
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' 3-2 overtime win Thursday against the Sabres isn't going to win any Emmy Awards. It was an objectively boring game for long stretches.</p><p>That's exactly what the Hawks hoped to accomplish, though, after a grueling week of reviewing and practicing how to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/09/blackhawks-systems-changes-jeff-blashill-wyatt-kaiser-defense" >tighten</a> their defensive structure.</p><p>After entering the week having allowed the most two-on-one rushes in the NHL, per coach Jeff Blashill, they didn't give the speedy Sabres any odd-man rushes of any sort. Their reads on the forecheck and in the neutral zone were clean and predictable, and they defended hard.</p><p>They didn't generate much offensively, either, and their offensive decision-making was considerably more suspect. </p><p>But their defensive structure allowed them to hang around until they scraped out something: a game-tying deflection goal by Frank Nazar with less than 12 minutes left, and a game-winning snipe by Ryan Donato three minutes into overtime.</p><p>"If you watch...a playoff game, for instance, there’s periods [or] half of games where nothing really happens," Ian Cole said. "It’s a boxing match. Of course, you want to land your punches, but you also don’t want to open yourself up to get tagged with a haymaker. There’s a give and take there, right? </p><p>"Being able to be patient while still waiting for chances, checking for your chances, that’s what a lot of good teams do. ... That’s good for us to see. That is a pattern that can work for us."</p><p>The victory snapped a six-game losing streak and improved the Hawks' home record to a respectable 5-5-0 with three more home games up next. Their dire road woes (0-8-1) are a problem for next weekend.</p><p>"The guys dialed in on their defensive details," Blashill said. "It was a real strong suit of the game."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Donato’s OT winner after the non-call on Frondell: <a href="https://t.co/XTagISqKkk">pic.twitter.com/XTagISqKkk</a></p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCST/status/2121087318778056935?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 13, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Caught a break</b></h3><p>Donato said he "felt terrible" as an illness came on, but his long-awaited goal — snapping a 10-game drought in which goalies had made a number of miraculous saves against him — put a smile on his face.</p><p>The Sabres were irate Anton Frondell wasn't whistled for interference for setting a pick on Owen Power, which gave Donato a ton of time and space. They had a strong argument. The Hawks probably caught a break, but they won't complain.</p><p>"We definitely needed something positive," Blashill said. "Confidence matters. Usually to come out of slumps like that, you have to grind your way. It’s never easy. </p><p>"We’ve obviously faced a lot of adversity through this last little stretch. Our guys, one thing I give them tons of credit on is they come to get better every day."</p><p>Blashill raved about Nazar, who not only scored both goals during regulation but also consistently drove play. The Hawks outshot the Sabres 9-1 during his five-on-five ice time.</p><h3><b>Got Kane back</b></h3><p>Patrick Kane returned to the Hawks' lineup after missing three games with an upper-body injury and looked rejuvenated. He remains goal-less since the season opener, but he had seven shot attempts Thursday and skated hard in both directions.</p><p>Kane didn't specify his exact injury but said he doesn't think it'll be a long-term concern. Hawks general manager Kyle Davidson said Wednesday the team doesn't think Bowen Byram's upper-body injury will be a long-term concern, either. </p><p>Byram has participated in practice — albeit while wearing a non-contact jersey — for the last two days. When he returns, it'll be interesting to see if he improves the defensive corps as much as the Hawks expect.</p><h3><b>More Blashill support</b></h3><p>Kane on Thursday joined the list of players who have spoken glowingly about Blashill recently. It shouldn't be surprising that the players aren't throwing their coach under the bus, but their quotes are still somewhat interesting.</p><p>"We have a lot of confidence in 'Blash.' He's a great coach, great communicator," Kane said. "I know he's a guy that can get the most out of his players. Right now, it's not working, so it's easy to look at the coach and blame the coach...but that's not the way we're looking at it. We have all the faith and confidence in management, ownership, Blash, the other assistant coaches.</p><p>"I always say some of the best parts of hockey, at least personally, is when you're struggling and you're going through tough times and you find yourself out of it, and then all of a sudden you start catching some momentum and start flowing after that."</p><h3><b>Another forecheck key</b></h3><p>There's a lot that goes into successful forechecks that fans (and reporters) often don't notice. Arriving at the right time and in sync with teammates, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/12/blackhawks-need-more-andrew-mangiapane-forecheck" >as Andrew Mangiapane recently discussed</a>, is one key.</p><p>Another key: Putting the puck in the right spot when dumping it in.</p><p>"It's definitely not as easy as I think people would think," Jordan Greenway said Wednesday. "You've got pressure on you, probably, when you're dumping it. You've got to either put it short of the goalie or it's got to go by him. You see a lot of pucks go to the goalie, right? It's not that easy. But you've got to do it."</p><p>The Hawks got burned Saturday, for instance, when Hurricanes goalie Pyotr Kochetkov was able to jumpstart a breakout against a poor forecheck. Avoiding the goalie is important. So is identifying which teammate has speed racing into the zone.</p><p>"[You look for] whoever can get to the puck quickest," Greenway added. "[You're] trying to get it to speed, right? Where someone can pressure it, where it's going to be tough for them to make a play."</p><h3><b>No Kevin again</b></h3><p>Embattled young defenseman Kevin Korchinski was a healthy scratch for the 14th time in 19 games. Blashill clearly doesn't trust him, and Davidson seems OK with that.</p><p>"I don’t believe in putting my thumb on the scale to get a certain player in a role or a certain player in the lineup," Davidson said. "That’s up to the coaches to decide what is best for those players, both individually and then the team as a collective. I stay out of those [decisions]."</p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams stars in Cubs' PCA MVP video
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams starred in the Cubs' social media video celebrating centerfielder <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/12/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-nl-mvp-award-gold-glove-platinum-glove-home-runs-stolen-bases-40-40-season" target="_blank" >Pete-Crow Armstrong</a> winning National League MVP on Thursday night.</p><p>In the video, Crow-Armstrong stands at home plate and tosses a ball in the air. When he makes contact, the words he wrote on the ball are made clear — "Love you Chicago! — Pete"</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Around here, PCA means MVP. <a href="https://t.co/5qzeOaal3e">pic.twitter.com/5qzeOaal3e</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2121046180863807910?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 13, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>With his parents sitting the stands, Crow-Armstrong hits a ball that soars out of Wrigley Field and flies through Chicago and over the water of Buckingham Fountain. It clears Soldier Field and lands in as parking lot south of the stadium — into the front windshield of Williams, who was watching Crow-Armstrong highlights on his phone.</p><p>Williams pries the ball off the windshield of his SUV and takes out a pen. He modifies Crow-Armstrong's original message so it reads "MVPete 2026."</p><p>Willaims and Crow-Armstrong have been friends for years, attending each other's games and even going to Bulls and Blackhawks contests together.</p>

entries.title: Thanks for giving more people a chance to help an artist out
entries.summary: <p>Thanks to the Sun-Times, WBEZ and freelance writer Mark Guarino for the recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/10/26/music-fans-rally-to-support-dean-schlabowske-of-waco-brothers-after-leukemia-diagnosis" >article</a> about musician Dean Schlabowske's health crisis. My wife and I became aware of his situation a few weeks ago because of a post on the Mekons Facebook page. But this was the first mainstream media coverage that I'd seen. It puts a spotlight not only on Deano’s personal situation, but also the harsh reality that musicians and artists across disciplines lack an adequate safety net for addressing life-altering events like this. My wife and I have donated a couple of hundred dollars to the GoFundMe campaign, and we urge other local music fans to do so.</p><p>Dean has not only been a mainstay of the alt-country/Americana music community for decades, he holds the distinction of having been a huge presence in the wine business here in Chicago. He may be remembered by customers at Wine Discount Center (now Vin Chicago), Sam’s in Lincoln Park and his own shop on North Avenue. Vinophiles who benefited from his expertise over the years may also want to help out.</p><p>Godspeed Dean and to your wife, Jo. You two have a tough row to hoe. But there are many of us pulling for you.</p><p><i>Mark Stanley, Irving Park</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-370000" name="module-370000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Pritzker’s Texas two-step </h3><p>There are plenty of uplifting stories stemming from the midterm elections, as American voters repudiated the corruption, incompetence and just plain meanness of the current president and his minions. But for me, the one that stood out for delicious irony and well justified comeuppance was the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/04/gov-jb-pritzker-role-texas-gov-greg-abbotts-defeat-gina-hinojosa-james-talarico" >article </a>reported by the Sun-Times' <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/tina-sfondeles" target="_blank" >Tina Sfondeles</a>.</p><p>I knew that Texas Gov. Greg Abbott had been roundly defeated. But I didn't know that his defeat was assisted by the large donation Gov. JB Pritzker made to Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa. I well remember the busloads of poorly clothed, bewildered migrants that Abbott sent without notification to Chicago in the middle of winter. Basic human decency required our political leaders in the city and state to take care of these poor people. Not being possessed of basic human decency, Abbott was proud to demonstrate his cruelty to make political points with like-minded officials in Washington, D.C. Thank you, Gov. Pritzker for using your wealth to present this MAGA monster with the humiliating defeat that he so richly deserved — a defeat to a Latina, by the way. Thank you also, Ms. Sfondeles for pointing this out.</p><p><i>Jim Bruton, Avondale</i></p><h3>He can’t help himself</h3><h3></h3><p>Donald Trump claims the Oval Office, with his garish gold additions, is a <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-signs-proclamation-he-says-will-prevent-future-changes-to-oval-office-and-cabinet-room" target="_blank" >national monument</a> akin to the White House. We've seen how he's respected that true monument — the people's house — by destroying the East Wing for his ballroom. Trump poses there and at the reflecting pool, pushing aside the fact that he got us into a war that he can't navigate and an inflationary spiral that has hurt all Americans. It's doubtful if the midterm results will change his conduct. There's always a new low for our president.</p><p><i>Philip S. Witt, Northbrook</i></p>
entries.author: Letters to the Editor

entries.title: Republicans who want a future in politics may want to distance themselves from Trump
entries.summary: <p>After suffering an absolute drubbing in last week’s midterm elections, Republicans seem to have learned few lessons.</p><p>America was not subtle or ambiguous in its rebuke of President Donald Trump, MAGA and Republicans — no fewer than 30 incumbent House Republicans lost their seats, Senate Republicans lost eight seats and five states changed party control at the gubernatorial level, all to Dems. It was a bloodbath.</p><p>Republicans <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-6028080/voter-polls-midterms-demographics" target="_blank" >lost</a> many of the gains Trump had made in 2024, most notably among independents and Latino voters. Democrats won voters under 30 by a whopping 48 points; they won men for the first time since 2008; and they even tied with white voters. Dems haven’t won white voters in a presidential election since 1964.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6a0000" name="module-6a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>All of that should compel MAGA and the GOP to do some serious self-reflection. And yet, they seem farcically determined to have learned no lessons from the trouncing.</p><p>In Trump’s first postelection move, he fired White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and put in her place Stephen Miller, the odious architect of some of Trump’s most infamous — and unpopular — policies, from his Muslim travel ban to his family separation at the Southern border.</p><p>Then, Republicans made Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, the House minority leader, empowering one of the body’s most pugilistic and hard-line members, and, incidentally, someone who’s passed zero bills in his 20 years in Congress.</p><p>And finally, in what could have been a signal to his own voters that Trump was turning the page on his very unpopular war in Iran, Republicans refused to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who promptly went on to <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/11/politics/hegseth-reprimanded-guard-tomb-unknown-soldier" target="_blank" >embarrass</a> them at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.</p><p>Trump has further threatened to imprison Democrats for investigating Trump officials for corruption, and suggested UFC head Dana White become the next White House spokesperson.</p><p>So, things are not going great. But if Republicans insist on following Trump down this path of self-destruction, they may be facing more losses in 2028 that will be even harder to recover from.</p><p>A new <a class="Link" href="https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-11/Reuters%20Ipsos%20Post%20Election%20November%20Survey%20Topline.pdf" target="_blank" >Reuters/Ipsos poll</a> reveals just how unpopular Trump and his acolytes are, if Republicans bothered to care.</p><p>Only 44% of Republicans view Trump very favorably, while 36% view him somewhat favorably.</p><p>A majority of Republican voters want the GOP’s next presidential candidate to “take a different approach to governing than Trump.”</p><p>If he was hoping to pass on the torch to his son, 43% of Republican voters said that Don Trump Jr. would be a “poor candidate,” while just 12% said he’d be “excellent.”</p><p>Just 34% said Vice President JD Vance would be “excellent.” As for others, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who would have to give up the only Republican Senate seat Texas has left to run, only had 10% say he’d be “excellent,” while 43% said former MAGA shill-turned-skeptic Tucker Carlson would be a “poor” candidate.</p><p>These are hardly rousing endorsements for the current Republican bench, or for the vibes MAGA is currently putting out.</p><p>We’ve learned over a decade that Trump is never chastened in defeat, and in his sunset years as an embattled lame duck, he’ll probably only get crazier and more sabotaging.</p><p>But for Republicans who hope their political futures outlive his, they may want to reconsider doing more of the same after voters — Republican voters, in many cases — said “enough.”</p><p>Maybe they shouldn’t follow Trump off the cliff. Maybe now’s the time to say no to the taxpayer-funded vanity projects, no to the war, no to more tariffs, no to the self-dealing and family corruption, no to the pointless political retribution, no to the reckless and humiliating Cabinet appointments, and instead focus on solving problems for Americans, something Republicans haven’t done in a very long time.</p><p>Maybe they should finally say no to Trump’s suicide pact, and yes to moving on — if only so that they can get elected again.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d10000" name="module-d10000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: S. E. Cupp

entries.title: Midterm elections shattered the MAGA hamster wheel
entries.summary: <p>Though last Tuesday's smashing Democratic victory was unlike anything we've seen in our lifetimes, perhaps the most striking thing is that on the morning after, it all felt so reassuringly normal. The election went forward at all 78,000 polling places. Hundreds of thousands of election workers and volunteers did their jobs. Citizens did theirs. No Immigration and Customs Enforcement goons loitered menacingly at polling places. There was no declaration of a state of emergency. There were no significant claims of cheating, undocumented immigrants voting or late-night ballot dumps. The speaker of the House didn't contrive a way to avoid certifying the victors. No major lawsuits were filed. The polls seemed to be more or less correct.</p><p>The victory speeches, at least the ones I saw, were gracious, and the concessions rapid and unambiguous. As the Noah-level flood engulfed Republicans, Donald Trump was asked whether he would accept the results. He said yes. (Though he has, more recently, begun to suggest otherwise.)</p><p>This is not the America we've been forced to live in for the past decade. It more resembles the country we feared we had lost just two years ago. For me, the most moving scenes Tuesday night were the temporary memorials to Alex Pretti and Renee Good festooned with "I Voted" stickers. The movement to preserve American democracy has martyrs now — and it has millions of adherents. Or does it? We'll come back to that.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9c0000" name="module-9c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>First, though, we deserve some joy along with the relief, and the electorate provided that in spades. The voters freed this country from what has felt, for many years now, like a doom loop. We seemed permanently polarized, trapped in a never-ending cycle of close elections decided by a few swing states, gerrymandered up the wazoo, consuming different news, seemingly living in different realities and goaded by demagogues into senseless hatred. The 2026 election shattered that hamster wheel. True reform is now possible. And some of the worst political actors got what they had coming.</p><p>Vivek Ramaswamy, who managed something that no other Republican (despite some valiant efforts) has been able to achieve — namely, to go lower than Trump — was defeated by 8 points in the Ohio gubernatorial race. Elon Musk, who moved to Texas to savor its MAGA musk and spent $450 million attempting to elect the felonious, election-denying philanderer Ken Paxton, was handed his hat (the politest formulation).</p><p>Trump's handpicked candidate in South Carolina was defeated by the physician Annie Andrews after a campaign in which MAGA coined the oh-so-witty nickname "Tranny Annie." Bo French, the GOP candidate for the influential Texas Railroad Commission, had the sort of bigoted history that has become table stakes in the Republican Party. In 2023, he posted an online poll asking who was a bigger threat to America, "Muslims or Jews?" In March, he declared that the United States should deport a hundred million people. In September, he followed up with an image of cheering University of Texas football fans who had a bit too much melanin for his taste. "Americans have been displaced by foreigners," French whined. He was "displaced" on the commission by Democrat Jon Rosenthal, who had the support of Republicans Karl Rove, Fort Worth Mayor Mattie Parker and George W. Bush (who somehow woke up from a decade's snooze). Also in Texas, Brandon Herrera, a YouTube something-or-other who showed off an original copy of Mein Kampf and bragged about membership in the Sons of Confederate Veterans, was defeated for Congress by Katy Padilla Stout.</p><p>You could go on all day — Greg Abbott is gone, along with Scott Perry (one of the architects of the Jan. 6 attempted putsch). Lauren Boebert joins her rival, Marjorie Taylor Greene, on the outside. And for poetic justice, it's hard to beat Scott Colom's story. A successful Mississippi prosecutor, Colom was nominated for a federal judgeship by President Joe Biden. One of Mississippi's senators, Roger Wicker, raised no objection (by tradition, senators can block nominees from their states). But the other, Cindy Hyde-Smith, refused to issue the required blue slip, and thereby blocked Colom's nomination.</p><p>It's a new day, but let's think about whether the results represent a total rejection of Trumpism. As much as I'd like to believe that, I'm afraid we've seen too much in the past 10 years to conclude that with confidence. Americans reelected Trump despite his 2022 call to "terminate" the Constitution to return him to office; despite Jan. 6 and his approval of the mob that attempted to murder his vice president; despite his cordial meeting with a neo-Nazi; despite his theft of highly classified documents; despite his tragic mismanagement of the pandemic that included idiotic musings about injecting bleach; despite his embrace of QAnon cranks; despite his corruption; despite his admiration for Vladimir Putin; and despite his promise of mass deportations.</p><p>Americans were OK with all of it until it pinched their pocketbooks. Since the start of Trump's second term, I have rooted for the tariffs to be implemented fully because I figured that that was the only way to make a large majority regret what they'd done in 2024. Voters needed to touch the stove, as they say. I didn't anticipate the Iran debacle, which taught the same lesson.</p><p>It's a new day, but Trump's actions and statements in the immediate aftermath of the election should not be misinterpreted as signals of any sort of mellowing. Stalin hid in his dacha for a while after Hitler invaded Russia. Sometimes autocrats need time to lick their wounds. No, Trump can soothe his eggshell ego by rationalizing that Republicans can't win without his golden name — a claim he made on Tuesday night — despite declaring for the previous four weeks that he was on the ballot. Still, he won't lead a mob to the Capitol on behalf of his party. That would be extending himself for others. He doesn't do that.</p><p>It's a new day, but we've learned in the past 10 years that key segments of American society do not uphold the law or even basic decency. Trump 2.0 could not have taken the dark turn that it did had key institutions in American society not enabled it. Yes, tens of millions of Americans did reject MAGA and all its ugly works, but they were not a majority in 2024.</p><p>Are they now? Probably not. The majority sent a message that it hates the high prices, hates the poorly conceived and arguably illegally waged war in Iran, hates the overreach on immigration enforcement (while liking the closed border) and hates the corruption.</p><h3></h3><h3>Building on the anti-Trump backlash</h3><p>Democrats seem to have gotten that message loud and clear, but without the White House, their capacity to make policy is limited — at least for now. Much of what they accomplish before 2028 will be signals of the direction a Democratic government would go. One hopes that most will join Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton in supporting the repeal of most of Trump's tariffs, though that will require some Democrats to abandon an earlier hostility to free trade. They should jump at it. Reducing tariffs is one of the only ways to bring down prices without a recession. And Trump has done Democrats the favor of convincing more than 60% of voters that tariffs are bad. In January, Congress can pass legislation repealing the president's broad tariff authority.</p><p>Ending the war on immigrants is not only the right policy morally, it's also practical. Home prices have risen in part because undocumented immigrants represent a significant share of homebuilders. Meatpackers have also been decimated by ICE raids. Trump promised to deport the worst of the worst but instead hounded the hardworking and law-abiding. The result was shameful human suffering and scarcer, pricier new homes combined with higher food prices. Once again, Trump has set the table for Democrats by convincing voters that mass deportation is both a moral stain and a practical disaster. Another layup for Democrats (provided they keep the border under control).</p><p>Now the challenge will be to solidify the anti-Trump backlash into permanent reforms that will insulate us from a return to strongman rule.</p><p>Fortunately, the Democrats' majority is large enough that we can entertain serious reforms like amending the Constitution to limit the president's power. One place to start is the limitless pardon power, which permits a lawless president to order subordinates to do illegal acts. Another is a constitutional amendment overriding the presidential immunity decision Trump v. United States. Impeachment turned out to be a failure. Constitutional amendment, perhaps?</p><p>But above all, we must remind ourselves, perhaps with better civics classes and more focused attention in the culture, of the preciousness of the rule of law, federalism and accountability. Nov. 3 was a great day for the Democrats. It can yet be a turning point in stabilizing our 250-year-old nation.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of the Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-040000" name="module-040000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: Mona Charen

entries.title: Bears CB Kyler Gordon is back from the depths of injuries: 'I still haven’t shown my true potential'
entries.summary: <p>When <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> hired Dennis Allen as defensive coordinator early in 2025, the only player he mentioned by name was nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon. Allen’s creativity ran wild with all the ways he could use such a savvy, multi-talented piece, and it looked like a perfect match.</p><p>But Gordon had been just as excited, and likewise was just as disappointed by the delay as he dealt with various injuries.</p><p>“It sucks because, in my career, I still haven’t shown my true potential,” Gordon told the Sun-Times. “I talk about it with my friends all the time: There’s a lot of stuff for me to show, and in this defense with D.A. over the next couple years, I’ll have a chance to do that.”</p><p>He missed 14 games with three injuries last season and had a calf injury in the recent offseason that kept him out of spring practices, training camp and the first five games.</p><p>Throughout, the Bears’ public coldness toward him exacerbated a frustrating ordeal for both sides. Coach Ben Johnson quickly moved to the next topic whenever Gordon’s name came up, and general manager Ryan Poles said going into the season he didn’t know whether he’d ever play for the Bears again.</p><p>That turned the temperature up on Gordon within the fan base. It became popular — and wildly off-base — to call him the new Nate Davis, the offensive lineman who signed a big contract with the Bears but appeared to lose his passion and has been out of the league since the team cut him midseason two years ago.</p><p>They’re not the same at all. Being away was miserable for Gordon, who called it “a daily mental battle.” The process was made harder, he said, because of “really having the environment around you be not what you’d think it would be.”</p><p>When asked whether he was saying the Bears were unsupportive, Gordon simply repeated the line and laughed. It was notable that after a historic performance in his return last month, he posted an old video clip of Poles clapping on Instagram.</p><p>Gordon was unbelievable <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/18/bears-cb-kyler-gordon-goes-off-with-3-sacks-in-return-from-injury-everything-i-wanted" >that day against the Falcons</a>. He got three sacks, stopped star running back Bijan Robinson for a loss and forced two fumbles in just 17 snaps. He is believed to be the first defensive back in NFL history with three sacks and two forced fumbles in a game.</p><p>With Gordon finally fully healthy, everyone saw what he and Allen dreamed of, and Gordon reminded everyone he’s one of the league’s premier nickels. He can cover anyone from slot receivers to tight ends, he’s a playmaker against the run, he can shift outside when needed and he’s the best blitzer there is.</p><p>In four games, Gordon has four sacks, 13 tackles and a pass breakup, and quarterbacks have a collective 86.6 passer rating when throwing his way. He said his goal is 10 sacks this season, which would set the record for a defensive back.</p><p>The contentiousness has subsided, too, as his play has drawn compliments from Poles, Johnson and Allen over the last few weeks.</p><p>If Gordon can stay on the field, his partnership with Allen will be the most dangerous part of this defense other than the ever-present possibility of defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons busting into the backfield. And Allen’s style is much more in line with Gordon’s mentality than former coach Matt Eberflus’ was.</p><p>“We’re constantly threatening people or attacking people and making the offense make a quick decision, rather than being conservative and having people attack us and seeing what happens,” Gordon said. “I like his mindset as far as being on the attack and on the hunt and let them fear us.”</p><p>His uncanny blitzing ability fits that philosophy perfectly, and his versatility makes him a deceptive weapon for Allen.</p><p>The Bears had been one of the league’s most blitz-happy teams under Allen, though that’s not his preference to help their struggling pass rush. That’s already declined since trading for Simmons.</p><p>That only makes Gordon more unpredictable for opposing offenses. Allen can create uncertainty by presenting him as a blitzer, then drop him back into coverage. Or, he can be opportunistic about turning him loose.</p><p>Gordon has been an acrobatic athlete for the Bears since they drafted him in the second round in 2022 and earned the nickname Spiderman because of that and his ability to save a play at the last moment.</p><p>But it’s the mental side that makes him elite. Gordon he processes and stores information like a computer. His rookie season, for example, was a bumpy ride as he got burned by veteran quarterbacks like Aaron Rodgers, but rather than be derailed by those failures, Gordon simply took them as data to help him improve.</p><p>When he talks about his approach to blitzing, it’s almost all intellect.</p><p>“Awareness is such a big thing,” Gordon said. “That’s why I appreciate my God-given ability to learn and retain it all when I go out there. I’ve studied so much and I’m so aware of all the possibilities that could happen and what I’m going to do.”</p><p>Gordon’s return, followed by Simmons’ arrival, was crucial to the defense’s improvement. Even if he still feels some resentment, the ironic part is the best way for him to stick it to the Bears is to be exactly what they want: a game-changer at the center of their defense.</p><p>If he keeps playing like this, he’ll reestablish himself as an essential piece. He’s in the first season of a three-year contract extension that Poles offered him thinking he’d be a cornerstone, and if he stays on this course, the unpleasantness of the past year or so will fade into a footnote.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Dear Abby: Sibling who did time fibs about marital status after partner’s death
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> A family member, "April," recently lost her partner. Although I deeply disliked the individual, I was able to muster an "I'm sorry" when he passed. Then, April started posting how long they'd been married. (They weren't married.) If her timeline is accurate, then he would have been with her at the state women's prison, where she was incarcerated in the early 2000s.</p><p>I know I should keep my opinions to myself, and I did resist pointing out the error. If she wants to forget that period of her life, that's OK, but what if she is dishonestly trying to extend their time together for financial gains from his estate? Should I correct her before an attorney does? — <i>NOT A MARRIAGE</i></p><p><b>DEAR NOT A MARRIAGE:</b> April may be trying to ease her pain by fudging the facts — a lot. If that's all it is, leave well enough alone. However, if you truly believe she's planning to commit estate fraud, it's your duty to speak up. There's no need to embarrass April publicly, but do share what you know with the executor of her partner's estate.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have a parent who thinks they should know everything about everybody. If I get something in the mail, they will read it to see what it's about. If I go shopping, they want to look at everything I bought. If I take out the trash, they want to know what's being tossed. Today, they asked somebody how much their employer is paying them! If I don't tell them everything, they say I'm being rude.</p><p>Family and friends have expressed displeasure about the way this parent acts. Is there something that can be done to help them see it is not necessary to know everything? — <i>NO PRIVACY</i></p><p><b>DEAR NO PRIVACY:</b> While parents do need to keep tabs on their minor children's activities, the behavior you have described is over the top. Have you tried proactively overloading this person with a lot of boring details about your day? If they get the impression that your life is uninteresting, they may stop hovering. Above all, do not let your anger show when they get nosy. If you do, it will only reinforce the suspicion that there's something they need to know.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My wife and I go out to dinner twice a month with another couple. Over the years, we have split the bill down the middle. Unfortunately, they order expensive entrees, bottled water, drinks and desserts that we do not. As a result, we end up subsidizing their meals, and our bill is often between $150 and $200. It's getting harder to afford.</p><p>How can I suggest separate checks without implying that they eat too much or spend too much? Because that is how, I'm afraid, it would sound. — <i>GOING BROKE IN THE WEST</i></p><p><b>DEAR GOING BROKE:</b> Do not make this about the other couple. Simply say casually that it would "work better for us if we got separate checks." That way there will be no shaming involved, just a simple statement of facts.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Evanston musician Jason Narducy is back with more tales of rock ’n’ roll in ‘Mostly the Van’ part two
entries.summary: <p>Jason Narducy would be the first to tell you that rock ’n’ roll stories are not all biting the heads off bats, snorting human ashes, setting hotel rooms on fire and having some intern pick out all the brown M&Ms in your dressing room.</p><p>Sure, the Evanston-reared musician has his “Behind the Music” sagas from touring with Bob Mould, Superchunk and the R.E.M. covers project with Michael Shannon. There’s also his own musical projects Split Single, Verböten and Verbow. But the tales he chooses to share in glorious detail in the second volume of his memoir series “Mostly the Van” (out Nov. 17) are a bit more innocuous. Like, getting Facebook friend requests from George Wendt, sparring with Guided By Voices’ Bob Pollard over Miller Lite vs. Heineken and playing with his band Split Single at the infamous Pizzagate restaurant in Washington, D.C., around the time the 4chan conspiracy went viral in 2016.</p><p> And there is one unbelievable story about the time he was in Paris with the band Telekinesis and, fresh from a dire tourist trip to the underground catacombs, he witnessed a motorcyclist catch on fire.<b>  </b></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-070000" name="module-070000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Jason Narducy Book Release Show</h3><br><b>When:</b> 6:30 p.m., Nov. 15<br><b>Where:</b> SPACE, 1245 Chicago Ave., Evanston<br><b>Tickets:</b> $20-30<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://evanstonspace.com/" target="_blank" >evanstonspace.com</a></div> </div><p>Still, Narducy said, “I think most people in the general public think that if you are in the music industry, you're either famous or you're a hobbyist, when actually there are tens of thousands of us in here that make a living at music. Those are the stories that interest me the most. … I wanted a human thread.”</p><p>The tone is set straight away with the book title. It references a time in 2023 when Narducy was on the road again with fellow musician Kieran McCabe, and as they set foot in a Midwestern coffee shop, the barista immediately knew they were in a band. But not by reading cues of their thrifted duds or sniffing out their rock star <i>je ne sais quoi</i>. No, it was “mostly the van,” as she told them, referencing their beat-up sprinter outside the café windows. Plenty more humble brags ensue in the book.</p><p>With such a long touring pedigree, Narducy has plenty of stories, which made it easy to fill a second volume, nearly a year after the first was released last December. Both are on the indie imprint Porchlight Books and edited by former musician turned publishing pro, Freda Love Smith (once of alt rock group Blake Babies), who helps give the book its sharp insider edge. Photos including self-captured Polaroids, some very early iPhone snaps and the work of professionals also fill the pages. That includes two happenstance shoots with a random van outside photographer Nathan Keay’s North Side house that helped capture the essence of the book title. (Narducy donated his trusty set of wheels, Old Bessie, years ago.)</p><p>“When I was driving to [Nathan’s] house for another photo shoot, the van was still there — a year later,” Narducy said, dumbfounded. “I want to leave a note for that guy or that gal and just say, ‘Thank you. [Your van] is in a bunch of books.’” </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-190000" name="image-190000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/984daf0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F13%2F4c%2F6ffc17714fae8c7b705315d56c70%2Fprotestsongs-260726-015.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b547c82/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F13%2F4c%2F6ffc17714fae8c7b705315d56c70%2Fprotestsongs-260726-015.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b6495b3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F13%2F4c%2F6ffc17714fae8c7b705315d56c70%2Fprotestsongs-260726-015.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Jason Narducy sits in SPACE music hall in Evanston, Tuesday, July 21, 2026. Those are the stories that interest me the most. … I wanted a human thread,” Narducy said of the latest volume in his memoir series.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But it was going back to his teenage days, around the time when the North Shore teenage punks Verböten were making waves, that sets Narducy’s latest collection apart. In the pages, there are modern-day run-ins with Dave Grohl and his mom Virginia (“Ginny” as Narducy calls her), referencing how the Foo Fighters frontman grew up with Verböten singer Tracey Bradford and credits the young group for inspiring him to write songs.</p><p>The book also starts with 19-year-old Narducy getting a call at his day job at Record Exchange on Belmont Avenue and finding out he was going to be a father. It ends with his first-born daughter, Alexa (then 8), brushing off Narducy’s “very challenging” gig singing the national anthem at a Bulls game in 2000. “I think almost every parent can relate to having a kid who just does not care about anything they do,” the musician jokes.</p><p>But the crown jewel of adolescent tales in the book, without giving too much away, involves Narducy getting yelled at by late sportscaster Tim Weigel (the stepdad of one of his high school friends) for playing music too loud and then getting caught in the crosshairs with Evanston PD for some illicit activity in Dawes Park.</p><p>“I was like, this is the first time I’m submitting a story that's not music related. But [Freda] said, ‘I don't know, you going toe to toe with the Evanston Police Department at age 17 is pretty rock ’n’ roll,’” Narducy said with a laugh. “It taps into that kind of teenage rebellion, a rare moment where … the cops were f------ with us, and we won.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p> A grown-up Verböten famously reunited in 2024 with gigs at Riot Fest as well as Metro and Salt Shed, respectively opening for Frank Black and Iggy Pop. There are no plans at this point for the group to keep going. </p><p>“I'm in so many bands and sometimes the schedule picks up,” Narducy said. Next, he and Shannon are booked on a 40th anniversary celebration of R.E.M.’s “Document” album this spring. </p><p>“But I hope that there's more shows,” he said, adding, “I really need to do a whole Verböten chapter!” </p><p>Narducy is sure there will be more van chronicles to come. “I have no question that there's two more volumes,” he says. “I also haven’t talked [fully] about Bob Mould, who is probably the most important [collaborator] I've had in my career.” But, Narducy said, he wants to wait a few years, gather more stories, find some perspective and of course make more music, like a new Split Single album that’s in the works. At a book event at SPACE on Nov. 15, following a conversation with “Daily Show” co-creator Lizz Winstead, Narducy will also reunite with Alison Chesley (his partner in Verbow) for a special performance of their Jason & Allison project, and who knows where that could lead, too.</p><p>If there’s one moment of mistruth in “Mostly the Van (Volume Two),” it’s Narducy talking about needing to think of a retirement plan at some point. In reality, he admitted, “I have no plan. … I’m really fortunate that I love what I do.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago mayoral candidates make their pitches -- and take aim at Brandon Johnson
entries.summary: <p>More than half of the candidates vying to become Chicago's next mayor gathered Thursday night in Lake View to launch the 2027 campaign just nine days after the midterm election. </p><p>A forum held at Temple Sholom on the city's North Side and moderated by Rabbi Shoshanah Conover featured 10 of the 16 candidates who filed petitions for mayor last month.</p><p>Each candidate was initially given two minutes to answer questions on public safety, education and antisemitism, though that was later cut to one minute as the large panel quickly ate up time.</p><p>Notably absent was incumbent Mayor Brandon Johnson, who was at a community budget town hall in Uptown at the time. So was Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias, who has been a fundraising powerhouse as his focus shifted to a run for mayor.</p><p>Chicago Public Schools was an early point of contention, with former state counsel Bill Quinlan taking the first shot at Johnson while suggesting closing under-enrolled schools and renovating or building new ones to operate more like “rec centers.”</p><p>“I don’t want to close the schools, I want to fill the schools,” U.S. Rep. D-Ill., Mike Quigley quipped back, saying he wanted to push for the creation of 50,000 affordable homes in underserved neighborhoods across the city.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> entries.title: Chicago police aren't going after domestic abusers' guns despite state law
entries.summary: <p>When her abusive ex-boyfriend pointed a gun at her head this summer, Dominique says she knew she had to do something before it was too late.</p><p>So she went to court<b> </b>and requested a protective order to keep her ex away from her and a search warrant for the police to go get his gun. She was able to do so under <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/02/10/gov-pritzker-karinas-bill-signing-firearms-domestic-violence" >Karina’s Law</a>, an Illinois law that took effect last year in an effort to protect survivors of domestic violence.</p><p>“I just don’t want to die,” the 26-year-old mother told a Cook County judge in September.</p><p>Her requests were granted. And the Chicago Police Department was sent a search warrant, which officers had 96 hours to execute.</p><p>But that didn't happen. Instead, a cop was back in court two days later to ask the judge to drop the warrant, according to a transcript of that hearing.</p><p>The officer argued that too much time had passed since Dominique last saw her ex-boyfriend’s gun, saying that made it difficult for police to “conclusively say that that firearm remains in the location.”</p><p>Dominique says she was shocked.</p><p>But to those tracking the implementation of Karina’s Law, the move was hardly surprising.</p><p>Since the law took effect, Chicago police have gotten at least 91 Karina’s Law search warrants, according to documents obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times. Only three have been served.</p><p>A police spokesperson says it's a safety issue for the police.</p><p>"Our focus is on recovering weapons from domestic violence offenders in the safest manner possible for all individuals involved," the spokesperson says, adding that some guns are still taken during arrests or when suspected abusers hand them over after a warrant is issued. </p><p>But advocates for domestic violence victims say the department is flouting the law and placing survivors at risk.</p><p>Dominique, who agreed to be interviewed on the condition she be identified by only her first name because she fears for her safety, questions when the police “will take it seriously.”</p><p>“What would it take?” she says. “Would it take [being] harmed or a fatal incident? God forbid those incidents occurring.”</p><h3><b>Questions raised on the honor system</b></h3><p>Karina’s Law was the culmination of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/07/23/domestic-violence-deaths-spiked-illinois-last-year-passage-karinas-bill" >a yearslong legislative battle</a> over how to crack down on abusers who own guns. It took effect statewide on May 11, 2025 — Mother’s Day.</p><p>The law was named for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/7/14/23794078/karina-gonzalez-protection-from-her-husband-shot-to-death-2-weeks-later" >Karina Gonzalez</a>, who was shot to death in July 2023, weeks after she told police she had been threatened by her husband, Jose Alvarez. Her 15-year-old daughter, Daniela, also was killed.</p><p>Gonzalez had been granted a protective order that barred Alvarez from possessing a gun. But his weapon was never taken away.</p><p>At the time, domestic violence survivors had the ability to request firearm removal when they sought an order of protection. But advocates say that enforcement was inconsistent and often inadequate.</p><p>Karina’s Law was presented as a solution. Now, judges granting an order of protection also can issue a firearm search-and-seizure warrant to law enforcement.</p><p>If the survivor has recently made a police report, officers have 96 hours to execute the warrant. If not, the police have 48 hours to investigate and raise any issues with a judge.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5a0000" name="image-5a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8ce19b4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3071+0+288/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F09%2Ff0%2F0e2deea6d601e1e4cb4b6eed2933%2Flittlevillage-07xx23-005.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/380a192/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3071+0+288/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F09%2Ff0%2F0e2deea6d601e1e4cb4b6eed2933%2Flittlevillage-07xx23-005.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d8980e8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3071+0+288/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F09%2Ff0%2F0e2deea6d601e1e4cb4b6eed2933%2Flittlevillage-07xx23-005.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A memorial for Little Village resident Karina Gonzalez and her 15-year-old daughter, Daniela, at 2611 S.
