entries.title: Where to ice skate in Chicago and the suburbs 2026
entries.summary: <p>With the season’s first snowflakes potentially <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/11/09/brief-gush-of-much-colder-air-may-usher-in-first-snowflakes-of-season-for-chicago-area-friday" target="_blank" ><u>falling on Friday</u></a>, it’s a sign that now is the time to hit the rink.</p><p>Whether you have your sights set on Olympic glory or don’t know a snowplow from a salchow, one of these 14 Chicago-area venues, from great date night spots to large, regulation-sized rinks, offer something for skaters of all levels. At Skatium Ice Arena in Skokie, you’ll even find classic rink fare like burgers and nachos with Jamaican flair.</p><p>Several rinks in our list offer free admission if you bring your own skates; all of them rent skates for kids through adults. Hours of operation vary widely, and reservations are required by a few rinks. Classes for figure skating and hockey are on tap at many. Here’s where to lace up your skates in the Chicago area this season.</p><hr><p></p><h3> <a class="Link" href="https://www.blackhawksicecenter.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Blackhawks Ice Center</u></a></h3><p>1801 W. Jackson Blvd.; 312-455-7600<br>$12 admission; $6 skate rental<br><i>Year-round</i></p><p>You don’t need to be an avid Blackhawks fan to enjoy the year-round facility where the team practices. Located on the Near West Side, the Blackhawks Community Ice Rink offers regular public skates, freestyle skating drop-ins for the more advanced (you might even spot <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcsports.com/olympics/news/jason-brown-figure-skater-skate-america" target="_blank" >figure skater Jason Brown</a> practicing his routines as the Olympian has recently relocated back to Chicago after training in Toronto for several years) and hockey programs for kids and adults. If you are a Blackhawks fan, practices are also open to the public; check the <a class="Link" href="https://www.blackhawksicecenter.com/skate" target="_blank" >schedule</a> to line up your viewing in the same excursion. Reservations or presale tickets for public skate sessions are not required but all admissions will be on a first-come, first-served basis.</p><hr><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://rosemont.com/thepark/event/skating-in-the-park-5/" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Wolves Ice Rink</u></a></h3><p>5501 Park Place, Rosemont; 847-349-5009<br>Admission free; $8 skate rental<br><i>Nov. 29-Jan. 31, 2027</i></p><p>The Chicago Wolves Ice Rink returns to the 200,000-square-foot Parkway Bank Park entertainment complex, giving shoppers and skaters the chance to cross off both pursuits in one trip. Once you’ve finished showing off your layback spin and Axel jump (or just safely made your way around once or twice the rink without faceplanting), transition to dinner or catch a new release at the AMC Rosemont 12. The rink’s season kicks off on Nov. 21, when Rosemont’s mayor flips the switch on 80,000 holiday lights during the family-friendly event. Also part of the festivities are visits with Santa and Mrs. Claus, horse-drawn sleigh rides and carolers. Parkway Bank Park is accessible via the Blue Line; parking is free with validation. </p><hr><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.gallagherway.com/events/winterland-at-gallagher-way-2026/2026-11-20" target="_blank" ><b><u>Gallagher Ice Rink</u></b></a></h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Why is Chicago alderman the job few want? In February, 11 ward races will be uncontested.
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago City Council is more independent than it’s ever been, forcing Mayor Brandon Johnson to issue four vetoes, cast three tie-breaking votes, accept a Zoning Committee chair he did not choose and struggle to pass two budgets with mounting<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/11/10/city-council-aldermanic-opposition-letter-mayor-brandon-johnson-proposed-budget-revamp-demand" > resistance for a third.</a></p><p>Yet in spite of that transition from rubber stamp to real power, 11 wards are uncontested in the Feb.23 aldermanic election.</p><p>Ten incumbents are guaranteed re-election: Alds. Lamont Robinson (4th); Peter Chico (10th); Nicole Lee (11th); Ray Lopez (15th); Ronnie Mosley (21st); Samantha Nugent (39th); Andre Vasquez (40th), Anthony Napolitano (41st); Matt Martin (47th) and Debra Silverstein (50th). </p><p>They don’t have to raise a penny or spend a minute shaking hands, knocking on doors or attending neighborhood forums.</p><p>Neither does newcomer Elianne Bahena, chief of staff to — and handpicked successor of — retiring Ald. Michael Rodriguez (22nd).</p><p>Even more incumbents could end up running unopposed when the dust settles from petition challenges.</p><p>Other veterans are likely to face only nominal opposition from challengers with very little money. They include: Brian Hopkins (2nd); Pat Dowell (3rd); Desmon Yancy (5th); Monique Scott (24th); Felix Cardona (31st); Bill Conway (34th); Gilbert Villegas (36th); Nick Sposato (38th); Brendan Reilly (42nd); Timmy Knudsen (43rd) and Bennett Lawson (44th).</p><p>Chicago is closer than ever to the strong Council, weak mayor form of government the city code intended. And yet, only 140 candidates filed to run for City Council seats.</p><p>That’s down from 210 candidates filing nominating petitions to run for alderperson in 2023, 174 of whom ultimately survived petition challenges.</p><p>"It's possible that our constituents are pleased to see a City Council with teeth and a coalition of aldermen who are stepping up, doing the hard work and pushing back on the executive branch of government for the first time in many, many decades," said Reilly, a leader of the group that calls itself the "Common Sense Caucus."</p><p>"In other cases, maybe it's a job they simply don't want. There's so much upheaval at City Hall, perhaps some folks don't want to sign up for that circus."</p><p>Southwest Side Ald. Marty Quinn (13th), one of three veteran incumbents retiring from the City Council, is not surprised about the higher number of uncontested races. He ties the shortage of competition to the historic Nov. 3 election for 21 seats on Chicago’s first elected school board that preceded the 2027 aldermanic contests. </p><p>“Having these two election seasons intersect has taken a lot of potential aldermanic candidates off the table,” Quinn said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-180000" name="image-180000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0160353/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3251x1825+0+249/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd8%2F98%2F4e8792806fa38912c4ac0d220d09%2Fcouncil-061319-02.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b79b056/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3251x1825+0+249/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd8%2F98%2F4e8792806fa38912c4ac0d220d09%2Fcouncil-061319-02.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e7dc8fd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3251x1825+0+249/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd8%2F98%2F4e8792806fa38912c4ac0d220d09%2Fcouncil-061319-02.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Marty Quinn (13th) chose not to run again in the Feb. 23, 2027 aldermanic election." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e7dc8fd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3251x1825+0+249/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd8%2F98%2F4e8792806fa38912c4ac0d220d09%2Fcouncil-061319-02.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c39901c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3251x1825+0+249/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd8%2F98%2F4e8792806fa38912c4ac0d220d09%2Fcouncil-061319-02.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e7dc8fd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3251x1825+0+249/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd8%2F98%2F4e8792806fa38912c4ac0d220d09%2Fcouncil-061319-02.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ald. Marty Quinn (13th) chose not to run again in the Feb. 23, 2027 aldermanic election.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“People who are real active in the community, involved in schools, LSCs [local school councils], block clubs — those are the natural aldermanic candidates. And a good number of those [were] on the ballot” for school board.</p><h3>‘There’s so much negativity’</h3><p>Southwest Side Ald. Matt O’Shea (19th) who is calling it quits after four terms in the City Council, bemoans how the job has changed.</p><p>O’Shea blames that same sharp turn to the left — with seven Democratic Socialists serving alongside Johnson, the most liberal mayor in Chicago history — for turning off candidates who might otherwise find it attractive to seek a City Council seat.</p><p>“You have a career that you would be leaving to go into public service, and public service is so ugly. There’s so much negativity. There’s so much distrust,” O’Shea said. “And then, you go down to City Hall and you see people arguing about issues we have no control over, half-way around the world. I would guess that would turn off a lot of people.”</p><p> O’Shea can’t help but be surprised by the lack of interest in a job that will now pay $159,264 a year at the high end after the latest pay raise, which was tied to the rate of inflation.</p><p>“When you look at communities in crisis and you look at people elected in some of those communities and they don’t have opposition? That should be startling to people,” O’Shea said. “There’s no one in a community of 50,000 people who thinks they could do a better job or want to do a better job?"</p><p> </p><p>Mike Ruemmler, president of One Future Illinois, said he is not surprised that so many incumbents are running unopposed, and that the entire field of pre-challenge candidates is 66% of what it was four years ago. Ruemmler's group is a nonprofit created by business leaders to influence city and state policy, in part by electing a more conservative City Council. The group is planning to support several anti-administration Council members who seek to defeat as many as ten mayoral allies.</p><p>“People probably see the job and say, `Why would I want to do that? Why would I want that job?’ What about it would make somebody want it?” Ruemmler said. “It’s been a rough four years. A lot of rancor within the Council. Tough budgets to deal with. And it takes a lot to say, `I want to serve.’ It doesn’t seem like a desirable job to have these days.”</p><p>Lee is grateful for the vote of confidence at a time when she is fighting to keep the White Sox in the Bridgeport area and a planned Amtrak maintenance facility out of the Bridgeport community. Amtrak wants to relocate its South Loop rail yard to Bridgeport, and if that happens, Sox minority owner Justin Ishbia would like to build a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" >new White Sox ballpark </a>in Amtrak's old South Loop rail yard site. </p><p>Being an alderperson is "not a cakewalk sort of job as some people may have thought of it years ago, Lee said. "This is technically a part-time job. And when I talk to people about that, I tell them it's more like two full-time jobs."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-330000" name="image-330000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e57d9ef/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F25%2F32%2F67b9ea0d45f0b3b187c06b2552e7%2Fsoxstadiumfolo-260909-05.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4e06eea/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F25%2F32%2F67b9ea0d45f0b3b187c06b2552e7%2Fsoxstadiumfolo-260909-05.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d713bab/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F25%2F32%2F67b9ea0d45f0b3b187c06b2552e7%2Fsoxstadiumfolo-260909-05.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Nicole Lee (11th) joins dozens for a news conference outside Rate Field on the South Side Sept. 8. Speakers decried the proposed plan to move the White Sox out of Bridgeport and the construction of a 24/7 Amtrak maintenance facility." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d713bab/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F25%2F32%2F67b9ea0d45f0b3b187c06b2552e7%2Fsoxstadiumfolo-260909-05.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2c9c9eb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F25%2F32%2F67b9ea0d45f0b3b187c06b2552e7%2Fsoxstadiumfolo-260909-05.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d713bab/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F25%2F32%2F67b9ea0d45f0b3b187c06b2552e7%2Fsoxstadiumfolo-260909-05.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ald. Nicole Lee (11th) joins dozens for a news conference outside Rate Field on the South Side Sept. 8. Speakers decried the proposed plan to move the White Sox out of Bridgeport and the construction of a 24/7 Amtrak maintenance facility.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Violet Miller/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>The cost of running for alderman</h3><p>Veteran political consultant Delmarie Cobb ties the lack of interest to the cost of an aldermanic campaign. The days when you could run for a City Council seat by knocking on doors and “just being visible” are long gone, she said.</p><p>“It’s the gated communities. More and more buildings are locked. You can’t knock on doors. People aren’t answering their doors. They’ve got cameras out there. They see who it is. They don’t even come to the door. People used to volunteer for campaigns. They don’t do that anymore. So you have to spend the money,” Cobb said.</p><p>“The idea of getting $300,000 — where am I gonna get that? How am I gonna run a viable campaign if the incumbent chooses not to appear at forums, which might be my only possible opportunity to do a one-on-one where people can see a comparison?”</p><p>Cobb recalled what happened when she ran the 1999 aldermanic campaign that helped Ald. Anthony Beale (9th), who is now the City Council dean, unseat incumbent Robert Shaw.</p><p>“If it hadn’t been for the forums, there’s no way he would have won,” Cobb said of Beale. "Now a lot of incumbents refuse to do them with their opponents. They figure, `You can’t afford to really run against me, so why should I give you this unnecessary publicity.’”</p><p>Rodriguez is delighted, but not all that surprised, that nobody filed to challenge Bahena, his chief of staff. Bahena was the leading vote-getter in her down-ballot race for the local police district council and is “very well known” in the 22nd Ward, which includes Little Village and North Lawndale.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-040000" name="image-040000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0b42d58/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6010x3373+0+317/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F16%2Ff0%2F88eeafe3658a7b618f36273533f2%2Fcouncil-031623-36.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fd36777/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6010x3373+0+317/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F16%2Ff0%2F88eeafe3658a7b618f36273533f2%2Fcouncil-031623-36.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5247179/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6010x3373+0+317/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F16%2Ff0%2F88eeafe3658a7b618f36273533f2%2Fcouncil-031623-36.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Michael Rodriguez (22nd) pictured at a March City Council meeting." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5247179/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6010x3373+0+317/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F16%2Ff0%2F88eeafe3658a7b618f36273533f2%2Fcouncil-031623-36.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e28eeb0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6010x3373+0+317/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F16%2Ff0%2F88eeafe3658a7b618f36273533f2%2Fcouncil-031623-36.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5247179/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6010x3373+0+317/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F16%2Ff0%2F88eeafe3658a7b618f36273533f2%2Fcouncil-031623-36.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ald. Michael Rodriguez (22nd) speaks during a City Council meeting at City Hall in 2023. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“It’s good to be endorsed by Chuy Garcia and Mike Rodriguez in Little Village and the 22nd Ward. But it’s also the police district council, being my chief of staff and fighting for the community to the extent that the Gestapo detained her a year ago for seven hours,” Rodriguez said, a reference to federal agents carrying President Donald Trump’s deportation campaign. “She has a stellar resume and she’ll be the first female in that seat. I think that has kept people out.”</p><p>Nugent has managed to balance the demands of her Far Northwest Side constituents and navigate the outcry about the homeless encampment in a local park, while also helping to lead the 31-member bloc of conservative and moderate alderpersons who rejected Mayor Brandon Johnson’s corporate head tax last year and have threatened to do the same this year.</p><p>By maintaining that balance, Nugent believes she has earned the political pass.</p><p>“I’m a workhorse. I’m out in the community all the time. I love representing my community and the residents and families and I think they know I don’t take their support for granted,” Nugent said. “ Hopefully, no opposition just reflects that they know I’m there to support them.”</p><p>Vasquez, a former battle rapper once known for his homophobic and misogynistic lyrics, attributed the high number of uncontested races, including his own, to how much time City Council members are now spending on what he called “crisis management.”</p><p>“Maybe they understand how bad the budgets are looking,” Vasquez said.</p><p>Four years ago, five ward races were uncontested at the close of filing, but ballot challenges doubled that number to ten.</p><p>The open seat in the 21st Ward drew 14 candidates. Thirteen candidates vied for the vacant seat in the 6th Ward.</p><p>The modern-day record for candidates filing to run for Chicago alderperson was set in 2011, the year that Richard M. Daley’s retirement set the stage for the election of Rahm Emanuel. The field of 351 candidates filing for a Council seat was ultimately reduced to 239 candidates after petition challenges.</p><p>In 2023, the City Council welcomed 16 newly elected alderpersons, an unusually large turnover that followed a wave of retirements, resignations and defeats.</p><p>The lowest turnover in modern history occurred in 2003, when the freshman class included just three new members — Manny Flores (1st); Howard Brookins (21st) and Rey Colon (31st).</p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydhhaud-l-i/" target="_blank" >Sophie Sherry</a></h5><p><b>Watchdogs report</b>: Under Karina’s Law, domestic violence victims in Illinois can get a search warrant for the police to go after their abusers' firearms. But Chicago police have served just three of the 91 warrants issued since the law took effect last year, the Sun-Times found.</p><p><b>In practice</b>: Benna Crawford, managing director of Legal Aid Chicago, said that, since May, Chicago police have failed to execute any of the warrants issued in cases brought by more than 30 clients of her company. In almost every case, police officials returned to court and asked a judge to negate a warrant, Crawford said.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: A police spokesperson says it's a safety issue for the police. But advocates for domestic violence victims say the department is flouting the law and placing survivors at risk.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The law was named in honor of Karina Gonzalez, who was fatally shot in July 2023, just weeks after she told police she had been threatened by her husband, Jose Alvarez. Her 15-year-old daughter, Daniela, was also killed. Gonzalez had been granted a protective order that barred Alvarez from possessing a gun, but his weapon was never taken away.</p><p><a class="Link" album</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydhhaud-l-jk/" target="_blank" >Selena Fragassi</a></h5><p>The creation of Andrew Bird's 2005 album "The Mysterious Production of Eggs" developed over an arduous, yearslong journey with stops and starts that came during a time of "immense change and personal challenge," the Illinois-born musician told the Sun-Times.</p><p>In the beginning, Bird abandoned city life and built a studio in an 1890s barn his family owned in the northern Illinois village of Elizabeth. As he tinkered away at the lush jazz-folk-pop album, his audience was farm chickens, raccoons and a peacock.</p><p>Back then, the classically trained violinist lived in Uptown, taking gigs at the Green Mill and Hideout and teaching classes at the Old Town School of Folk Music. But Bird wasn't feeling totally fulfilled and desired to retool his career. Doing so took a process of "trying to rewire my brain," he said.</p><p>Eventually finished in L.A., "Eggs" became a hallmark of early millennium indie folk and set a precedent for Bird’s 17 whimsical albums and wide-leaping, award-winning compositional work that followed.</p><p>To mark the 20th anniversary of "Eggs," Bird reworked the songs into full orchestral arrangements and will perform the album in full symphonies nationwide. He's in Chicago on Friday and Saturday to perform with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, a kind of full-circle moment for the 53-year-old.</p><p>"I was in the Chicago Youth Symphony Orchestra, and I studied with Blair Milton, who was in the orchestra and at Northwestern [Bird's alma mater]. So, this is kind of a big deal for me," he said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydhhaud-l-ju/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>PICTURE entries.title: 'Hen-Dawg & Jimmy V' podcast – with 11-year-old Henry, 10-year-old Jimmy – isn't just kid stuff
entries.summary: <p>Ten-year-old Jimmy Maley was explaining the size of the guest room in his basement where he and 11-year-old Henry Zotti do their podcast.</p><p>“It’s probably around the size of like – obviously, you have a refrigerator,” Jimmy said this week. “It’s about 10, 12 of those.”</p><p>Apparently, that’s how kids today measure space, by its equivalent in refrigerators.</p><p>“Actually, it’s 18 refrigerators,” Jimmy said.</p><p>“That’s what he said?” Jimmy’s father, Jim, said later. “It’s way smaller than that.”</p><p>Whatever its size, the room in their La Grange home fills with silliness and seriousness during the “Hen-Dawg & Jimmy V” show, which gained national attention in September when Henry and Jimmy <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reel/DdWTN8slR91/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&exln=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==" target="_blank" >appeared on the “Today” show</a> after an NBC producer noticed them on social media.</p><p>It reached another level when “Today” <a class="Link" href="https://youtube.com/shorts/M2qsqIIz9ek?si=GwuAstfFOB_9w2vD" target="_blank" >surprised the boys with tickets</a> to the Bears’ game last Sunday on NBC’s “Sunday Night Football.” Before the game, they were on the sideline <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1de6HNCWYm/" target="_blank" >meeting quarterback Caleb Williams</a>, who already had been liking and reposting their videos.</p><p>“It was absolute cinema,” Henry said of their encounter.</p><p>The boys’ exposure had exploded even before Williams entered the picture. Many of their videos on Instagram and TikTok had been seen by millions. Their newfound fame helped them land interviews with Bears Hall of Famer Brian Urlacher and Cubs World Series hero Ben Zobrist – not to mention popularity in school.</p><p>“In the hallway, they’re like, ‘My, God, it’s the dynamic duo,’” Henry said.</p><p>“Yeah, they’re really nice. Always supportive,” Jimmy said.</p><p>In fact, the genesis of the show is all about support, specifically for Jim’s mental-health journey. Though the show elicits lots of laughs, its origin is deadly serious.</p><p class="cms-textAlign-center">*   * *</p><p>In 2003, Jim Maley was starting for Northwestern’s basketball team as a freshman forward. That’s an accomplishment in itself, but Maley wasn’t thinking that way.</p><p>“I was struggling bad with depression, but I didn’t know what it was,” he said. “And I just quit out of nowhere.”</p><p>Maley’s mother, Pat, convinced him to get help. When she died in 2018, Maley gave her eulogy and shared how Pat was his biggest supporter in his mental-health battle.</p><p>At the time, Jim and his wife, Katie, didn’t know anyone in their west-suburban community who struggled with mental health. After the funeral, which drew a packed house because of Pat’s popularity, Jim suddenly met many people who were struggling. They called, texted or approached him in public, thanking him for talking about it.</p><p>“That’s when I realized, I have to do this more,” said Maley, who had taken a leave of absence as the basketball coach at St. Laurence to tend to his struggle. “I was talking to individual students at the time, individual players when I saw them struggling. But that moment was when I knew, all right, I think I’ve got something here.”</p><p>Maley eventually began speaking publicly as a mental-health advocate. At Conant, where he now teaches part-time, school social workers were giving a presentation on mental health to each gym class. Maley asked if he could speak. Though they appeared hesitant at first, the social workers allowed it.</p><p>“I did it that first period, and they were like, ‘Can you do it the next seven periods?’ ” he said.</p><p>A couple of years ago, Maley began hosting his own podcast to discuss his mental-health experiences, which also included being hospitalized. Katie eventually joined to share her side of his struggles. Maley likened it to “an airing of grievances from ‘Seinfeld’ about marriage and parenting.”</p><p>One day, Henry approached Maley. He had struggled with anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Henry’s mom had shown him some of Maley’s clips, and Henry told Maley that he had some of those same thoughts. Henry asked if he could do a podcast with Maley, and they did.</p><p>Another day, Henry and Jimmy were bugging Maley to do their own podcast. Maley was hanging out with a friend, and to keep the boys occupied, he relented and set up the makeshift studio in the basement. He had planned to erase the pod the next day, but he listened to it first.</p><p>“I was like, ‘Holy you-know-what, this is funny,’” Maley said. “They were talking about sports like they actually have some pretty good knowledge. I just posted it on my feed thinking it would be funny for my buddies, that type of thing. And then it exploded.”</p><p class="cms-textAlign-center">*   * *</p><p>The boys’ first show was in May.</p><p>“It was about sports and food,” Jimmy said. “And we were yelling at our friend William. He’s a Packers fan.”</p><p>Talking into a microphone for people to hear isn’t easy, even for adults. What gives these two the confidence to do it?</p><p>“After we were on a couple of shows, we really got used to it,” Jimmy said.</p><p>“We got on a hot streak,” Henry said.</p><p>Henry went to his first Bears game Sunday. What did he think of it?</p><p>“It was absolute cinema,” he said.</p><p>What do the boys think of Soldier Field?</p><p>“I think it’s a classic,” Jimmy said.</p><p>“So do I,” Henry said, “and I don’t think we should ever change it.”</p><p>What do they want to do when they grow up?</p><p>“If I can’t become a great sports player, I think broadcasting’s my way to go,” Jimmy said. “I mean, I’m really good at it.”</p><p>“I want to be an NFL player and an NFL coach,” Henry said. “But if I can’t do that, I’m going to be a broadcaster for ‘Sunday Night Football.’”</p><p>Until then, they have shows to do.</p><p>“It’s been super fun, like, the whole ride,” Jimmy said. “And I don’t think it’s going to stop anytime soon.”</p><h3>Remote patrol</h3><p><b>Late Hicks was set to call BC-ND</b></p><p>The news of <b>Dan Hicks</b>’ death this week was stunning. He had been set to call Notre Dame’s game Saturday against Boston College in South Bend. That assignment now goes to Jason Benetti, who will join Jason Garrett in NBC’s booth.</p><p>But the broadcast will have solemn undertones in honor of Hicks, 64, who died of an “acute illness” Wednesday, according to Hannah Storm, his wife of 32 years. Hicks was a consummate professional known best for broadcasting golf, his favorite sport. He also called Olympic skiing and swimming and was on his second stint calling the Irish.</p><p>Hicks was in Chicago in September to call the Presidents Cup at Medinah and in October to support his daughter <b>Riley</b>, who ran the Chicago Marathon.</p><p><b>PA Sinclair talking a ton</b></p><p>It’s busy season for <b>Tim Sinclair</b>, the public-address voice seemingly for every team that <b>Gene Honda</b> isn’t. The Bulls’ game Wednesday capped Sinclair’s run of eight games in seven days.</p><p>He was in Champaign last Thursday for basketball and Friday for football. Last Saturday, he worked the Fire’s regular-season finale, and he had a Bulls-Bears doubleheader Sunday. On Tuesday, he worked the Champions Classic, a college hoops twinbill at the United Center.</p><p>Sinclair has become a fan favorite over the years for whomever he’s working. For the Bulls, he has continued the tradition of outstanding PAs, including <b>Ray Clay</b> and <b>Tommy Edwards</b>. Though he’s great for the Bears, many still have a fondness for <b>Jim Riebandt</b>.</p><p>Riebandt: “There’s a timeout … .” Fans: “Where?” Riebandt: “On the field.” Fans: “Oh.”</p>

entries.title: Cops release photo of man who bashed passenger in head with chair aboard Red Line on Near North Side
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police released pictures of a man wanted for hitting someone with a chair aboard a CTA Red Line train on the Near North Side earlier this week. </p><p>The attack happened around 3:45 p.m. Wednesday in the 1500 block of North Clybourn Avenue when a man believed to be between 40 and 50 years old struck a 25-year-old man who was a passenger in the back of the head with a collapsible chair, police said. </p><p>The man was last seen wearing a white and blue stocking hat, white jacket, navy blue jogging pants, and multi colored gym shoes, officials said.</p><p>Anyone with information is encouraged to call Public Transportation Detectives at 312-745-4447. <br></p>

entries.title: Ten players poised for breakout high school basketball seasons
entries.summary: <p>Even with what were very modest numbers, Deerfield’s Tommy Donahue was instrumental in helping Deerfield to a Class 3A state runner-up finish a year ago as a junior.</p><p>While he averaged just under seven points a game, he filled his role exceptionally well and most importantly made plays when they counted. But the 6-4 guard took off when the postseason began, emerging as a regular double-figure scorer as the Warriors reached the State Finals for the first time in program history.</p><p>“Tommy’s emergence, really starting with the regional championship game, kind of shifted our season,” said coach Jack DiMatteo, who takes over the program this year after being an assistant the past four years.</p><p>The confidence he gained in the state tournament run propelled Donahue. He turned in what was an ultra-impressive summer. There were multiple games in June where he drained eight or more three-pointers while he was a regular 20-point scorer.</p><p>“He really is a product of the work he’s put in,” DiMatteo said. “The coolest part is he doesn’t do it alone. He’s always bringing in teammates with him to work.”</p><p>The last few years the offensive strategy remained pretty simple: utilize Dartmouth-bound big man Jake Pollack to the fullest. The four out, one in offense was designed to do just that with Pollack in the high or low post.</p><p>But this year it will be more guard heavy. DiMatteo will rely on his perimeter players, setting up what should be a breakout season for Donahue, one of the premier shooters in the area.</p><p>While Donahue’s strength is his perimeter shooting, he will be both on the ball and off the ball for the Warriors, creating a versatile scoring threat for DiMatteo and matchup challenges for opponents.</p><p>“We will use Tommy as a playmaker with some ball screens while also creating open catch-and-shoot situations for him,” DiMatteo said. “He is capable of posting up smaller guards as well. This summer he showed a variety of ways that he can score.”</p><p>Donahue ended his recruitment this fall with a commitment to Division III power Washington-University in St. Louis. That makes Donahue one of the highest ranked City/Suburban Hoops Report players to go the Division III route.</p><p>Donahue’s overall numbers of 6.8 points a game and 36 made threes last season will skyrocket this winter. With what he showed this past offseason, Donahue is poised to be one of the true breakout players in the 2026-27 season.</p><p>Here are nine other prime breakout candidates this season.</p><h3><b>Kendall Meyers, Marist</b></h3><p>The defending state champs graduated four starters and six of their top seven players. That leaves a long, wide open runway for the lone returning starter. The 6-5 Meyers can play multiple positions and will continue to be a Swiss Army knife. But expect even more of an impactful scorer this season after averaging 7.7 points a game as a junior.</p><h3><b>Jamier Montgomery, Crane</b></h3><p>The show will revolve around the smooth scoring, Kent State-bound guard. But now as a senior he’s ready for it as he’s shown greater consistency, efficiency and confidence during the spring and summer circuit.</p><h3><b>Michael Woods, Perspectives-Leadership</b></h3><p>The biggest strength of this sleeper team could be the downhill force of Woods, who could be the biggest impact player in the Public League. The bucket-getting guard transferred back to the city from Don Bosco Prep in Indiana and may very well provide 20-plus points a night.</p><h3><b>Terrence Davis, Libertyville</b></h3><p>Thus far the injury bug has slowed the 6-2 junior down over the past year; Davis played just one game last season. But a healthy Davis will display his talent and explosiveness quickly and emerge as a big name in the Class of 2028.</p><h3><b>Ryan Whitt, Phillips</b></h3><p>This is a unique young player in the city. Whitt is a unknown sophomore with the strength and body to go with athleticism and emerging skill on the perimeter. Big numbers and an emergence awaits for the rugged 6-5 Whitt.</p><h3><b>Grant Smith, Lyons</b></h3><p>The feeling is Smith flew under the radar a bit last season when you consider he averaged 17 points a game as a sophomore. With a big productive year under his belt and plenty of recruiting steam, the athletic 6-6 Smith will be a game-changer this season.</p><h3><b>Dajuan Brown, Bradley-Bourbonnais</b></h3><p>An under-the-radar freshman season included leading the team in rebounding and assists while averaging 9.1 points a game. The 6-2 guard will break out as one of the top players in the sophomore class as Bradley-Bourbonnais will enjoy more success with Brown and three other returning starters.</p><h3><b>Noah Van Tholen, Riverside-Brookfield</b></h3><p>Van Tholen passes the look test with athleticism and outstanding positional size as a 6-3 point guard. Fresh off an impressive summer, Van Tholen could double his sophomore numbers of nine points and three assists a game.</p><h3><b>Orlando Bohlen, Payton</b></h3><p>Bohlen is only a sophomore, but he will firmly put his name on the radar this season after a freshman year where he quietly but impressively averaged 15 points a game. Even more remarkable? He’s a shooter who made 49 percent from beyond the arc a year ago.</p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson's chief financial officer abruptly resigns, third CFO to quit in a year
entries.summary: <p>The abrupt resignation on Friday of Mayor Brandon Johnson’s third chief financial officer in a year could trigger another drop in Chicago’s already shaky bond rating and scare investors away from the city’s bonds.</p><p>Ashlee Gabrysch's departure sent shock waves through City Hall and beyond — her resignation comes in the middle of a budget stalemate, after just three months as CFO. Even more damaging than Gabrysch’s sudden exit is what she said on her way out the door.</p><p>A former Wall Street executive, Gabrysch issued a statement saying she was unwilling to compromise her financial integrity. She did not reveal what it was she was asked to do that would have damaged her reputation.</p><p>“As the City of Chicago’s Chief Financial Officer, there is nothing more important than my fiduciary duty to the City and its taxpayers. The Chief Financial Officer’s statements about city finances are not idle chatter: they are relied upon by investors, ratings agencies, City Council, and taxpayers. The CFO must act scrupulously to ensure they are always accurate and complete,” Gabrysch said in a statement released to the media.</p><p>“Throughout my career, I have remained committed to upholding the highest standards of financial integrity and transparency, and in my short time as Chief Financial Officer, I have faithfully discharged this duty. It has become apparent, however, that to continue in this role would be to compromise my integrity and professional obligations. I therefore have concluded that I must step down from my role, and hereby tender my resignation.”</p><p>Finance Chair Pat Dowell (3rd) demanded an outside audit of the city’s finances in response to Gabrysch's resignation.</p><p>Gabrysch had replaced Steven Mahr, who himself had abruptly resigned, along with his top deputy, just days before veteran Budget Director Annette Guzman followed both men out the door. Gabrysch had previously served as senior director and mid-central region manager at Fitch Ratings. Since 2019, she had worked as Fitch’s lead analyst for both Chicago and Illinois.</p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: Illinois customers to receive payments from $63 million Family Dollar settlement over price discrepancies
entries.summary: <p>Illinois customers will soon receive payments after Family Dollar agreed to a $63 million settlement over allegations of price discrepancies at its stores, officials announced Friday. </p><p>Illinois, the Federal Trade Commission and 16 other states sued the company, alleging it charged customers more at the register than the prices advertised on store shelves, price tags and in advertisements.</p><p>The company will have to establish a $40 million redress fund for eligible consumers and a $20 million discount program for customers, Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul said in a Friday statement. </p><p>Illinois will also receive $188,548 in the settlement.</p><p>“Family Dollar overcharging for products at a time when many basic necessities have become less affordable harms vulnerable families and communities,” Raoul said in the statement. “I am pleased with this settlement that holds Family Dollar accountable and takes steps to ensure that it will not overcharge consumers in the future. I remain committed to protecting Illinois consumers from unfair business practices.”</p><p>The complaint alleged that thousands of Family Dollar stores overcharged customers and that the company failed to address the problem despite repeated failed inspections and customer complaints.</p><p>Family Dollar will be required to post notices of the redress fund at all stores and on its digital platform, Raoul's office said.</p><p>The chain must also establish a pricing accuracy program that will regularly monitor and verify prices, train employees to identify discrepancies, and correct errors to ensure customers are charged the prices advertised or displayed.</p><p>The pricing accuracy program will be independently assessed and certified annually.</p><p>Family Dollar did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p>
entries.author: Cindy Hernandez

entries.title: Bulls sign center Orlando Robinson from NBA G League affiliate Windy City
entries.summary: <p>The Bulls signed center Orlando Robinson from their NBA G League affiliate, Windy City, on Friday to fill their 15th and final standard-contract roster spot.</p><p>With a full roster, the Bulls' two-way players — Tobe Awaka, Jordan Hawkins and Jaylin Sellers, who split time with Windy City — are eligible to play in 50 games each, rather than 90 combined. The Bulls have been using their two-way players, particularly Hawkins, who has played in five consecutive games. </p><p>Robinson averaged 13.7 points and eight rebounds for Windy City in three games. He also played in three preseason games for the Bulls, averaging 6.3 points and 4.3 rebounds per game.</p><p>The 26-year-old Robinson has appeared in 115 NBA games over four seasons, playing for the Heat, Kings, Raptors and Magic. Robinson, who debuted with the Heat in 2022, has career averages of 4.6 points, 3.8 rebounds and 1.2 assists in 13.3 minutes. </p><p>Robinson played three college seasons at Fresno State, where he scored the second-most points in school history (700). He entered the NBA as an undrafted free agent.</p><p>Robinson will wear No. 00.</p>

entries.title: NFL quarterback power rankings: Where does Bears QB Caleb Williams land among 32 current starters?
entries.summary: <p>A ranking of NFL quarterbacks would’ve humiliated <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> as they wandered through Mitch Trubisky, Justin Fields and others before drafting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a> in 2024. Now, with Williams hitting his stride, it’s promising.</p><p>The Bears believed he could change the course of their franchise, and general manager Ryan Poles compared him to Patrick Mahomes. Williams still has a long way to go, but he’s having his best season even after throwing four interceptions against the Buccaneers last week.</p><p>As the NFL starts the second half of its season, here’s where all 32 starters stand:</p><p><b>1. Joe Burrow, Bengals</b></p><p>Burrow’s prominence faded after missing nine games last season, but leads the NFL in passer rating (114.8), completion percentage (74.0) and touchdown passes (23).</p><p><b>2. Josh Allen, Bills</b></p><p>Allen is doing his usual MVP-caliber work as a passer, but also chasing his own record for quarterback rushing touchdowns (15) with nine.</p><p><b>3. Brock Purdy, 49ers</b></p><p>Purdy’s efficiency is hard to top. He’s never had a season with fewer than 65% of his passes completed or a passer rating below 96.</p><p><b>4. Jared Goff, Lions</b></p><p>It’s another clockwork season for Goff, who has his second-best passer rating at 106.4 and is now 54-35-1 as the Lions’ starter.</p><p><b>5. Trevor Lawrence, Jaguars</b></p><p>Lawrence has been the league’s most accurate thrower, per Pro Football Reference, with nearly 84% of his passes graded as on-target.</p><p><b>6. Patrick Mahomes, Chiefs</b></p><p>Coming off a torn ACL, Mahomes looks back to normal. He’s had just one bad game out of eight in his return.</p><p><b>7. Jordan Love, Packers</b></p><p>Love averages nearly 300 yards and just had a monster game against the Patriots: 23-for-29 passing, 372 yards, three touchdowns, 153.2 passer rating.</p><p><b>8. C.J. Stroud, Texans</b></p><p>What a comeback: Stroud has been answering questions about his dropoff the last two seasons and whether he’s the Texans’ future.</p><p><b>9. Caleb Williams, Bears</b></p><p>Williams hasn’t arrived, but is arriving. Establishing himself as the best quarterback from his 2024 draft class is a key mile marker.</p><p><b>10. Jayden Daniels, Commanders</b></p><p>It’s been two seasons of injuries and inconsistency after his huge rookie year, but there’s still plenty to like about where he’s headed.</p><p><b>11. Dak Prescott, Cowboys</b></p><p>Prescott has been trending downwardly for three seasons now and might need a change of scenery if he wants to do some real winning.</p><p><b>12. Matthew Stafford, Rams</b></p><p>The Rams are back above .500, but need more from the reigning MVP. He already has thrown more interceptions (nine) than last season (eight).</p><p><b>13. Drake Maye, Patriots</b></p><p>Maye is among the best young quarterbacks, but has thrown a league-worst 11 interceptions and has four games with a sub-80 passer rating.</p><p><b>14. Geno Smith, Jets</b></p><p>No one notices because he plays for the hapless Jets, but Smith is having one of his best seasons at age 36.</p><p><b>15. Kirk Cousins, Vikings</b></p><p>The Vikings saw their ship sinking under terrible quarterback play and turned to Cousins to save them. He was playing solidly for the Raiders.</p><p><b>16. Bryce Young, Panthers</b></p><p>Young has been all over the place this season, and that shouldn’t be happening in Year 4. The Panthers should start over.</p><p><b>17. Tyler Shough, Saints</b></p><p>After a good rookie season, Shough has progressed modestly. The Bears get a look at him next weekend coming off their bye.</p><p><b>18. Aaron Rodgers, Steelers</b></p><p>Rodgers hasn’t been elite since 2021, but he’s holding it together well enough for the Steelers to be 6-2 atop the AFC North.</p><p><b>19. Deshaun Watson, Browns</b></p><p>It’s hard to believe the Browns are 5-4 and harder still to believe that Watson is back to playing at even a decent level.</p><p><b>20. Jacoby Brissett, Ravens</b></p><p>Brissett is a journeyman on his seventh team, but he’s stepping into an advantageous situation with Lamar Jackson potentially out for the season.</p><p><b>21. Sam Darnold, Seahawks</b></p><p>Darnold is out this week with a rib injury, but expected back for Seattle’s next game. He’s running out of time to get rolling.</p><p><b>22. Bo Nix, Broncos</b></p><p>The warning signs on Nix were always there, and it’s reached a point that he’s holding the Broncos back and they must reevaluate.</p><p><b>23. Michael Penix, Falcons</b></p><p>Much like Young, Penix has been erratic. Sometimes he looks like he could win a playoff game, other times he’s a wreck.</p><p><b>24. Justin Herbert, Chargers</b></p><p>Herbert has plunged, and the winless Chargers have gone with him. He’s been sacked 31 times in by far his worst season.</p><p><b>25. Baker Mayfield, Buccaneers</b></p><p>Coming off a three-year, $165 million contract extension, Mayfield hasn’t looked right since dislocating his thumb on his throwing hand.</p><p><b>26. Cam Ward, Titans</b></p><p>How can anyone even get a good read on Ward amid the total mess the Titans have been during his two seasons?</p><p><b>27. Daniel Jones, Colts</b></p><p>It’s tough to keep the job playing as poorly as Jones, who has a league-low 68.9 passer rating and is averaging under 200 yards.</p><p><b>28. Fernando Mendoza, Raiders</b></p><p>The No. 1 overall pick and Heisman Trophy winner will be the starter over the final eight games after the Raiders traded Cousins.</p><p><b>29. J.J. McCarthy, Giants</b></p><p>It’s rare to see a playoff team down here. The Giants’ playoff outlook would be much different if Jaxson Dart hadn’t gotten hurt.</p><p><b>30. Carson Beck, Cardinals</b></p><p>The Cardinals, already a mess, are on their third quarterback and it’s Beck, a third-round pick out of Miami, debuting against the Rams.</p><p><b>31. Joe Milton, Eagles</b></p><p>Milton is on his third team in three seasons, and the once-mighty Eagles are in freefall after losing starter Jalen Hurts.</p><p><b>32. Kyle McCord, Dolphins</b></p><p>McCord will start at least the next four games, and Dolphins starter Malik Willis’ return from a groin injury is uncertain.</p>

entries.title: Lurie Children’s gets state approval for $480 million hospital in Downers Grove
entries.summary: <p>Lurie Children’s Hospital of Chicago received state approval this month to build a $480 million pediatric hospital and outpatient center in Downers Grove, paving the way for the health system’s first inpatient hospital outside its Chicago campus.</p><p>The Illinois Health Facilities and Services Review Board approved the hospital’s certificate of need application on Nov. 5, a key step toward expanding pediatric emergency and specialty care in the western suburbs.</p><p>The proposed 298,000-square-foot facility will include 48 inpatient beds, an emergency department, operating rooms, diagnostic imaging and outpatient services. It is also expected to offer specialty care in oncology, cardiology, gastroenterology and orthopedics.</p><p>Lurie Children’s said the project is intended to make specialized pediatric care more accessible to families in the western suburbs, many of whom currently travel outside their communities to receive treatment.</p><p>“Every child deserves access to the specialized care they need, as close to home as possible,” Tom Shanley, the hospital’s president and CEO, said in a statement.</p><p>The hospital plans to begin site excavation in December, pending the release of permits by the village of Downers Grove. It expects to see its first patients in spring 2029.</p>

entries.title: Previewing the top IHSA football playoff quarterfinals
entries.summary: <h3>Class 8A: No. 4 Mount Carmel at No. 1 Lincoln-Way East, 1 p.m. Saturday</h3><p>Based on the teams' talent and resumes, this matchup feels more like a semifinal or even state final. But losses to East St. Louis and Brother Rice dropped Mount Carmel (9-2) to a No. 8 seed and here we are. Brady Cloherty, who started the season as the Caravan's No. 2 quarterback, already has set the program's single-season record for touchdown passes, aided by the state's deepest receiving corps. That group includes Michigan commit Quentin Burrell, Marshaun Thornton and Ty Kennedy. Mount Carmel's defense has stars at all three levels with lineman Caleb Tucker, linebacker Roman Igwebuike (Notre Dame) and defensive back Tavares Harrington (Michigan). All Lincoln-Way East (11-0) has done is win, with signature victories against Brother Rice, Kankakee, Homewood-Flossmoor and more. The Griffins beat Oak Park and Hinsdale Central the past two weeks with backup quarterback Tyler Sychalski filling in for Evan LeFevour.</p><h3>Class 8A: No. 7 Bolingbrook at No. 8 Oswego, 5 p.m. Saturday</h3><p>This is a rematch of Bolingbrook's 21-7 win in Week 4. A season-opening shutout loss to Homewood-Flossmoor is just a distant memory for Bolingbrook (10-1), which is led by two of the state's top players in running back TJ Lewis (Oklahoma State) and edge Darreion Prescott (Notre Dame). Lewis had one of the plays of the year in last week's 22-14 win against Lyons, a zigging and zagging 73-yard run that took him from one sideline to the other. Oswego (10-1), last year's Class 8A runner-up, is succeeding thanks to its usual mix of swarming defense and effective running by Ammar Banire, quarterback Drew Kleinhans and fullback Luke Hernandez.</p><h3>Class 6A: No. 23 Wheaton North vs. No. 21 Fenwick, 1 p.m. Saturday at Triton</h3><p>Wheaton North (8-3) is coming off the biggest upset in the playoffs, a down-to-the-wire 36-35 win against Geneva that avenged a 42-14 loss in Week 7. Sophomore quarterback Grant Neibch, who was promoted to the varsity in Week 6 after his older brother Burke went out with a hand injury, threw the game-winning TD pass to Johnny Clayton with 7.8 seconds left. Iowa recruit Jake Thies, arguably the best two-way player in the state as a running back and defensive back, has a program-record 44 career touchdowns and counting for defending Class 6A champ Fenwick (8-3).</p><h3>Class 5A: St. Francis at No. 25 Cary-Grove, 1 p.m. Saturday</h3><p>Defending 5A champion St. Francis (7-5) is one of two five-loss teams still alive (Nazareth is the other). Since losing to Montini in Week 9, the Spartans have averaged just over 50 points in three lopsided playoff wins. Running back Tivias Caldwell Jr., quarterback Jadon Wilson, receiver Greg Bess-Henning and two-way star James McGrath (Western Illinois) are among St. Francis' playmakers. Despite coming into the season with one of coach Brad Seaburg's least experienced teams, Cary-Grove (9-2) is in the quarterfinals for the seventh time since 2018. Quarterback Jackson Berndt has the Trojans' trademark triple-option offense humming along.</p><h3>Class 3A: No. 6 IC Catholic at Byron, 2:30 p.m . Saturday</h3><p>This could wind up being the de facto Class 3A title game. IC Catholic (10-1) has lost only to 8A power Loyola in a game the Knights led at halftime. Running back Jakobe Baldwin has rushed for more than 1,500 yards with 17 touchdowns and Grant Bowen, a top-40 player nationally in the junior class, has more than 800 receiving yards with 11 TDs. Byron (11-0) won last year's meeting between these two teams 28-6 en route to its third state title since 2021. The Tigers have an average winning margin of 45 points this season.</p>

entries.title: FAA grounds flights nationwide, causing delays and cancellations at O'Hare, Midway
entries.summary: <p>The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon following a communication issue between air traffic control centers. </p><p>An FAA alert said the stoppage was "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."</p><p>Ground stops were issued at Chicago O’Hare International Airport and Midway International Airport. As of 5:30 p.m., O'Hare had reported 328 flight cancellations and 847 delays. Midway saw 30 cancelled flights and 186 delays, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.flychicago.com/business/media/delays/pages/default.aspx" target="_blank" >Chicago Department of Aviation</a>. </p><p>U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communication issue affected all of the nation's 22 air traffic control centers that route planes between airports.</p><p>Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no sign yet that "this was a nefarious attack against us. It's just a telecommunications outage."</p><p>“Everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying,” Mullin said.</p><p>Prospect Heights residents Matt and Patricia Kowalski arrived at O’Hare two hours early for their annual holiday trip to visit family in Poland, prepared to board a flight to Germany.</p><p>He learned through the radio on their ride to the airport that a ground stop had occurred, so they decided to wait it out.</p><p>By 5 p.m., they had already missed their connecting flight and were debating waiting another three hours for the technical issues to pass in the hopes they could keep the trip going.</p><p>“Maybe we go back home tonight,” Matt said. “There’s no update now.”</p><p>There is no timeline for restarting flights. Mullin said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But that system operates out of one location near Washington, D.C., and just sends recommendations to the air traffic control centers.</p><p>The FAA's first alert went out shortly before 3 p.m.</p><p>The FAA, in a separate statement, said the ground stop was issued "out of an abundance of caution. "Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case-by-case basis," the FAA said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Friday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times<br></p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Nashville resident Paul Lindsay was on his way to Mason City, Iowa, with friends before learning of the ground stop at O'Hare.</p><p>"This is nuts," said Lindsay. "It's good to know this is not our problem. Every person in an airport in the United States is running into this problem."</p><p>The Chicago Department of Aviation said it had no comment and directed questions to the FAA, which did not immediately provide further details.</p><p>American Airlines, in a statement, said flights already in the air would continue to their destinations. "We expect disruption to our schedule for the rest of the day, depending on the length of the FAA’s nationwide ground stop," the company said.</p><p>This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.</p><p>The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year, according to the AP. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country. </p><p>But much work remains, the AP reported. Duffy has said that another $30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it.</p><p>The FAA recently expanded its use of an AI tool that reroutes flights at O'Hare, though there is no indication that the system is related to the ground stop. The system, called Strategic Management of Airspace Routing Trajectories, or SMART, has been used in Washington, D.C., since September. </p><p>But the FAA this week said it is now being used at O'Hare to reduce delays. The system has been used to reroute 180 flights across the country, the FAA said. Duffy has said the AI tool would offer recommendations to human air traffic controllers, who would remain in control of rerouting flights.</p><p><i>This is a breaking news story. Check back for updates.</i></p><p><i>Contributing: Associated Press</i></p>

entries.title: Speaker Chris Welch’s office hires law firm to assess Illinois House culture after sexual harassment scandal
entries.summary: <p>Outgoing Illinois House Speaker Emanuel "Chris" Welch, D-Hillside, has enlisted a Loop law firm to evaluate workplace culture in his chamber, following intra-caucus outrage over his delayed response to sexual harassment allegations that will soon force him to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/05/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-mutiny-26-democrats-call-for-new-leader-harry-benton-scandal" target="_blank" ><u>relinquish the gavel</u></a>.</p><p>The Prinz Law Firm received a $450,000 contract that began Sept. 21 to help assess and address Springfield’s entrenched culture of harassment, state records show.</p><p>A spokesperson for Welch’s office said they “retained the Prinz Law Firm in September to assess culture within the office and make recommendations for improvements. Their process is ongoing."</p><p>Attorney Kristen Prinz noted her firm was “not engaged to investigate any particular issue but rather to help the Office of the Speaker and the Clerk assess and improve the workplace culture.”</p><p>“We will be gathering feedback from staff and recommending policy and process changes to further trust, engagement and productivity,” Prinz said in an email. “We are grateful to be a part of this effort towards making work better for the people who serve our state.”</p><p>Welch came under fire over the summer after a legislative inspector general’s report confirmed the three-term speaker was aware of a complaint against ex-state Rep. Harry Benton almost three years before additional accusations prompted the Plainfield Democrat to resign.</p><p>In between, Welch put $1.4 million behind Benton’s reelection campaign, later claiming he had no choice but to support a member because the initial complainant declined to file a formal complaint.</p><p>Welch — who has faced allegations of misconduct himself <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/11/12/illinois-house-speaker-emanuel-chris-welch-accusations-domestic-abuse-lawsuits-patronage-proviso-district" target="_blank" ><u>over the years</u></a> — has since expressed regret over the way he handled the case, and he apologized for social media interactions with the complainant that made her uncomfortable.</p><p>Welch established a House culture and accountability working group to tackle the broader issue, but that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/05/welch-benton-harassment-working-group-cassidy" target="_blank" ><u>wasn’t enough</u></a> for an insurmountable bloc of Democrats who publicly announced last week they wouldn’t support him for a fourth term as speaker. He soon announced he’d step aside from the post while remaining a rank-and-file lawmaker.</p><p>Welch’s predecessor, Michael Madigan, was ousted from the speaker’s office amid complaints over his inaction on sexual harassment allegations, too, before the longtime ex-speaker’s ultimate downfall on a federal corruption conviction.</p><p>In a message sent to Democratic lawmakers and staffers, Welch’s office said the outside firm’s review is “intended to be as independent as possible” and that he “will not be directing it or otherwise managing it.”</p><p>“We believe a strong, inclusive, and respectful workplace culture is essential for everyone’s success and long-term growth. And we understand that is an ongoing process that needs to be regularly evaluated and updated,” Welch’s office told members.</p><p>Several Democrats are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/06/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-steps-down-female-replacement-contenders" target="_blank" ><u>jockeying to succeed Welch</u></a> as speaker, with maneuvering expected to intensify next week as lawmakers return to the Capitol for the fall veto session.</p>

entries.title: How Blackhawks rookie Anton Frondell keeps friendship alive with Jets' Viggo Bjorck
entries.summary: <p>Almost every day, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> rookie Anton Frondell, Jets rookie Viggo Bjorck and Islanders rookie Victor Eklund's three-man group chat blows up with messages.</p><p>"We three are best friends, so we're texting back and forth," Frondell said Friday. "We give each other energy."</p><p>Friday was likely one of the chat's quieter days, however, because Frondell and Bjorck — plus Bjorck's dad — were able to get dinner together in Chicago.</p><p>And on Saturday, the chat will be dead, because Frondell and Bjorck will be playing each other at the United Center. The three Swedes' deep friendship gets turned off for about three hours whenever two of them face off.</p><p>"We're enemies for the day," Frondell said. "[I] probably won't use that group chat. I'll just try to stay in my focus, my bubble. [But] outside of the ice, we're best buddies. I feel like that's pretty normal, though."</p><p>This will mark Frondell and Bjorck's second NHL meeting after years of developing side-by-side — along with Eklund — within the Djurgardens organization in Stockholm. The Hawks won the first matchup Oct. 15. </p><p>As long as they both remain in the Central Division, they'll see each other plenty. Frondell already <a class="Link" href="https://www.theelmonters.com/p/victor-eklund-anton-frondell-sweden-islanders-blackhawks-nhl-bjorck" target="_blank" >faced Eklund</a> on Oct. 8 in New York, too. The triangle will be completed next Thursday when Eklund's Islanders visit Winnipeg.</p><p>For the Jets, that Oct. 15 overtime loss in Chicago began a nine-game losing streak after a 4-1-1 start. Then a dramatic comeback Nov. 3 in Montreal flipped their fortunes again, so they enter Saturday riding a five-game winning streak.</p><p>Their upturn has coincided with Bjorck moving from center to wing. That's particularly interesting because the Hawks, by contrast, have been very reluctant to do the same with Frondell.</p><p>The Jets picked Bjorck eighth overall in June to address a massive organizational need for centers, but he — perhaps unsurprisingly — struggled to find immediate NHL success at that position. </p><p>Through Nov. 3, he had zero points in 16 games, and the Jets had been outscored 9-2 during his five-on-five ice time. Since shifting onto veteran center Adam Lowry's line, he has tallied four assists and been a <a class="Link" href="https://www.winnipegfreepress.com/breakingnews/2026/11/12/swedish-sensation-finally-finding-his-groove" target="_blank" >plus player</a>, albeit in a small sample.</p><p>"He's going to end up back in the middle down the road somewhere," Jets coach Scott Arniel said Friday. "But for a young player, 18 years old, he's been really good without the puck."</p><p>Frondell, meanwhile, continues to navigate choppy waves as he attempts to play center — and handle matchups against elite opponents like Jets star Mark Scheifele — as a 19-year-old.</p><p>He has had some impressive games and moments, and it's easy to follow the Hawks' logic. They want him gaining maximum experience in the Jonathan Toews-type role they foresee him holding long-term.</p><p>But considering Frondell has recorded only three points in his last 12 games, and that the Hawks haven't found any well-suited wingers for the first-line role next to Connor Bedard and Roman Kantserov, it's odd they haven't even given <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/30/blackhawks-anton-frondell-role-ice-time-connor-bedard" >that idea</a> a try.</p><p>General manager Kyle Davidson said this week they might rethink things if Frondell was getting "steamrolled every night," but they believe he's holding up well enough to forge on.</p><p>Frondell himself obviously isn't worrying about his deployment, nor about his inconsistent box-score stats. He said he's proud of his recent hard work to improve at faceoffs and on the penalty kill.</p><p>At his apartment, he still hasn't figured out how to watch NHL games on TV — which, to be fair, is no simple task. He hears all important updates through the group chat, though, and it sounds like he has raved about his Chicago experience so far.</p><p>"He's told me it's a great city," Bjorck said. "He likes his teammates very much. I'm happy it's going well for him and he's found his way into the team. I'm just happy that he's happy."</p>
entries.author: Ben Pope

entries.title: Ex-Cubs skipper Joe Maddon on why baseball stopped loving him back
entries.summary: <p>Joe Maddon still meditates every morning — 10 to 15 minutes upon waking, in his bed, a pillow over his eyes, deep breaths, focusing on what he’d like to make of the day ahead.</p><p>The ritual lasted longer when he was still managing in the big leagues, which he hasn’t done since the Angels fired him 56 games into the 2022 season. At 72, the top item on his agenda these days is often a round of golf at the country club outside his hometown of Hazleton, Pennsylvania, where he plays with the same pals he’s had since childhood.</p><p>Even if Maddon has fewer urgent matters on which to ruminate than he did, say, as the Cubs were closing in on a curse-busting 2016 world championship, he remains a thinker, a feeler, a strong believer in intuition. In baseball terms, Maddon is still all about “the human element,” as he often put it, rather than bloodless, soulless data.</p><p>Which certainly is one of the biggest reasons the game he loves stopped loving him back.</p><p>“Yeah, it kind of did,” he told me. “That’s a good way to put it.”</p><p>At 54, Maddon managed the Rays to their first division title and the World Series and became a star. At 62, he helped bring the mother of all championships to the North Side, where he’d been received by fans and the organization alike as a sort of savior. By 65, he was in a lame-duck season with the Cubs, his relationship with the front office doomed by philosophical incompatibility. At 68, he got fired. No teams have come knocking on his door since, and by now there’s no discernible chance of that changing.</p><p>“What I do and how I do it, I don’t think it’s necessarily sought after anymore,” he said. “In today’s world, whether it’s baseball or the corporate world, experience is not necessarily sought after. What everybody’s looking for is a more controllable asset that they can then nurture in their own image and likeness. That’s what they like.</p><p>“When I was coming up, it was very important to have your own thoughts and ideas because the manager was more autonomous and had to set the direction for the organization both on and off the field. In today’s game, in terms of the hiring process, I don’t think that’s what anybody’s looking for. The way things are handled — pregame [decisions], how teams are put together, the way tablets are used and tech — it’s not going to change. Control beats experience, intuition and feel because those three words, these guys have never done that. When you say that to them, it’s like you’re speaking a different language.”</p><p>Maddon stays involved with the game as a favorite guest of MLB Network host Brian Kelly and with the “Book of Joe” podcast he does with writer Tom Verducci. He does corporate speaking engagements, a nice way to make a buck. He plays in golf tournaments and keeps in touch with former coaches and players.</p><p>He also still loves to feed people, a lifelong enjoyment for someone who grew up in the family-owned Third Base Luncheonette in Hazleton. For 20 years, Maddon has hosted “Thanksmas” meals at holiday time for community members experiencing homelessness. It started in Tampa, Florida, and expanded to Hazleton and Chicago. On Saturday, Maddon will be back to serve Italian and Polish food — his specialties — alongside staff and volunteers at the Care For Friends facility in Lincoln Park.</p><p>“I’d like to try to bring some dignity to people who may have lost some of their own personal perspective on things, just based on their lot in life and how tough it’s been,” he said.</p><p>Later this month, Maddon and wife Jaye will pile into their sweet, beloved ride, motor down to Florida and spend the winter months at an RV resort near the St. Petersburg Country Club, where they are members. Some things never change.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/12/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-nl-mvp-award-gold-glove-platinum-glove-home-runs-stolen-bases-40-40-season" target="_blank" >Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong wins NL MVP to cap all-time season of homers, stolen bases and defensive excellence</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/11/cubs-free-agents-mlb-offseason-left-field-right-field-catcher-ian-happ-seiya-suzuki-carson-kelly-miguel-amaya-pedro-ramirez-matt-shaw" >As Cubs chase pitching, how would they approach potentially replacing a third of their lineup?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Maddon’s baseball proclivities haven’t changed. He’d still pull Kyle Hendricks from Game 7 of the World Series when he did. He still defends his extreme use of reliever Aroldis Chapman in that series.</p><p>Some around the Angels will never wrap their brains around what Maddon did a couple of months before his dismissal, intentionally walking a hitter with the bases loaded and his team trailing by a run. Yes, the Angels ended up winning. A young writer asked Maddon after that game about the “analytics” of the move.</p><p>“Numbers are one thing; human beings are something completely different,” Maddon lectured, adding that it had “nothing to do with math.”</p><p>So what if the move made spreadsheets spontaneously combust?</p><p>There’s one current big-league manager with whom Maddon most closely relates, and that’s World Series winner, well-liked “oldster” and fellow born raconteur Pat Murphy of the Brewers, who is 67.</p><p>“I love the way they play,” Maddon said, “and I think the way they’re playing really reflects the sensibilities of Murph.</p><p>“I just talked about how hard it is for a manager to make an impact based on the overarching philosophies of front offices, but Murph is one guy who has found his way through that. They realize how important he is to their success. I’ll say it straight-up — that team does not win it with anybody else managing them.”</p><p>Maddon and Murphy have known and liked each other for decades. When Maddon managed against the Brewers as a Cub, he didn’t spend much time trading stories and yuks with then-Brewers skipper Craig Counsell. He and Counsell’s then-bench coach, Murphy, always sought each other out before games, though.</p><p>“He and I have a lot in common,” Maddon said. “The sensibilities are very similar.”</p><p>Same goes for the experience.</p><p>“That’s what you’re seeing when he’s sitting on the bench or in postgame conversations with the press or whomever, it’s just all the years of having done this,” Maddon said. “He’s able to slow it down. He always has something to draw back on that permits him to slow moments down, and that’s what he does really well. And in the game today, I think that’s the sort of thing that’s missed.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/fweYpF_iPdc?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Angels intentionally walk Corey Seager with the BASES LOADED!"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>
